articles.title: Updated MLB Playoff Bracket 2026, White Sox vs. Guardians ALDS Odds, Preview
articles.summary: The Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Guardians will renew their American League Central rivalry in the ALDS.
articles.body:
The Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Guardians will renew their American League Central rivalry in the ALDS.

The White Sox advanced to the ALDS on Wednesday with a wild-card round sweep over the AL West champion Houston Astros. It marked the first time since the 2005 World Series that the White Sox won a postseason series.

The ALDS will have a similar feel to the September series between the two sides in Cleveland in which the Guardians took two out of three games.

Cleveland, the AL Central champion, is the expected favorite in the matchup against the most inexperienced roster left in the AL bracket.

Chicago didn't display any fear over two games in Houston, and if its bats can remain hot, it will have a chance to keep its unlikely run going.

Money Line: Cleveland (-168; bet $168 to win $100); Chicago White Sox (+142; bet $100 to win $142)

Guardians Will Try To Ride Pitching To Series Win

Cleveland holds the edge in pitching in the matchup with the White Sox.

Gavin Williams, Parker Messick and Foster Griffin give Cleveland a solid trio to start off the series. Tanner Bibee or Joey Cantillo could throw in Game 4.

Williams is the best starting pitcher in the series. He struck out 248 batters in the regular season and he was excellent in September.

Cleveland is 1-3 in Williams' four starts against the White Sox this season. Williams allowed three earned runs or less in all of those defeats.

Williams does have nine or more strikeouts in five of his last nine starts and he's going up against a White Sox lineup that has a propensity to strike out in large numbers.

Messick recorded at least eight strikeouts in three of his four regular-season meetings with the White Sox. He hasn't allowed more than three earned runs in a start since June 29.

Griffin, a midseason acquisition from Washington, gave up 30 hits in 18.1 innings in September. He's not as much of a sure thing as Williams and Messick, but he can give Cleveland five or six solid innings in a start.

Williams will likely pitch Games 1 and 5, if the series gets that far. He struck out eight over six innings in his lone postseason start in 2025.

The White Sox do have familiarity with Cleveland's starters, but the Guardians haven't had trouble striking out the White Sox, which is concerning for the lower seed in this matchup.

Cleveland also owns the bullpen advantage with Cade Smith headlining that group.

Experience is also on the side of the Guardians, but that won't matter much if they don't win games against a team with a lineup in good form.

The White Sox at least have offensive momentum on their side entering the ALDS.

The Chicago lineup tore through the Houston pitching staff for 13 runs over the two games in the wild-card round.

That was an extension of a red-hot final week of the regular season in which the White Sox scored 41 runs.

If you go back further to the Detroit series that began on September 18, the White Sox have 73 runs in their last 11 games.

The White Sox did score 16 runs in their last series against Cleveland, so there has to be a bit of confidence going into Ohio for Games 1 and 2 that they can hit.

Most of the Chicago lineup worked its way on base in the two games against Houston. It didn't rely on big hits from one player to carry it through that series.

Of course, Munetaka Murakami and Miguel Vargas have to show up, but keep an eye on the bottom third of the White Sox order.

Chase Meidroth had a pair of multi-hit games and a three-run home in Game 2, Braden Montgomery had two hits in Game 1 and Colson Montgomery homered in the opener in Houston.

If the success continues from the 7, 8 and 9 spots in the order, the White Sox might have the right formula to spring an upset, or at least push the series to five games.

articles.title: White Sox Eliminate Astros, Box Score Stats, Highlights & Bracket After 2026 MLB Wild Card Game 2
articles.summary: The Chicago White Sox, for the first time since 2005's World Series title, have won a playoff series.
articles.body:
The Chicago White Sox, for the first time since 2005's World Series title, have won a playoff series.

The Pope's favorite team defeated the Houston Astros 7-3 on Wednesday, sweeping the Wild Card Round matchup and setting up a showdown against the Cleveland Guardians in the ALDS.

Below we'll break down the game's key stats and moments, along with the updated MLB playoff bracket

Game 2 couldn't have gotten off to a much worse start for the Astros, as five hits and two Houston errors led to the White Sox jumping out to a 4-0 lead and starter Hunter Brown getting chased less than an inning into the contest.

But the Astros slowly clawed their way back into the game.

Jeremy Peña homered in the bottom of the first, Cam Smith blasted a solo shot one inning later and Jose Altuve lined the 28th postseason homer of his career in the bottom of the fourth—putting him just one behind Manny Ramírez for the most in MLB history—cutting the deficit to 4-3.

The Astros appeared set to steal the lead in the bottom of the fifth, loading the bases with two outs for Altuve, but he lined out to right field to end the threat.

That would prove to be costly almost immediately, as Chase Meidroth blasted a three-run homer in the top of the sixth to restore Chicago's four-run advantage.

Up next for the White Sox is their divisional rivals, the Guardians, in the ALDS. Game 1 will be Saturday at 1 p.m. ET.

articles.title: Astros' big bats fail to come through as White Sox put finishing touches on wild-card sweep
articles.summary: All year, Houston's slug-happy lineup was able to compensate for its shoddy run prevention. But not in its two playoff games against Chicago.
articles.body:
The stage was set for the Houston Astros to once again overcome their deficiencies on the mound with their stars in the batter's box.

For the second day in a row, the Astros put themselves in an early hole against the Chicago White Sox in their American League wild-card series. In Game 1, it was rookie reliever AJ Blubaugh who imploded as the opening act of a wayward bullpen game , recording two outs and walking three before being replaced. Facing elimination on Wednesday in Game 2, it was Houston's best pitcher, right-hander Hunter Brown, who couldn't finish the first frame . He surrendered five hits and a walk to No. 9 hitter Colson Montgomery before manager Joe Espada trudged to the mound in a most unwelcome case of deja vu.

The deficit in Game 1 was 1-0 after the first inning. Game 2 was 4-0 White Sox before the Astros picked up the bats. But a trio of solo homers from Jeremy Peña , Cam Smith and Jose Altuve got the Astros back within one in a relative blink. And in the bottom of the fifth inning — having kept Chicago's bats quiet since the first — the Astros had something cooking against the White Sox bullpen.

The Astros had pushed White Sox starter Sean Burke 's pitch count up to 72 through four innings of work, prompting manager Will Venable to turn to right-hander Huascar Brazobán to begin the fifth inning, with the top of Houston's lineup looming. Brazobán allowed two of the first three batters he faced to reach base, bringing AL MVP favorite Yordan Alvarez to the plate with runners on first and second and just one out. Venable then summoned lefty Anthony Kay to face Alvarez, who went 1-for-4 in Game 1 and struck out against Burke in his first two at-bats of Game 2.

This was not only Alvarez's chance to make his mark on this series but also the familiar escape hatch the Astros had accessed all season. Their unreliable pitching staff — injury-ravaged but also ill-equipped to begin with — regularly required Houston's bats to bail them out. The Astros ranked 24th in MLB in ERA (4.45) but first in home runs (226), with Alvarez's 42 long balls leading the way. Time and again, Alvarez delivered, staying healthy for a career-high 158 games en route to humongous production unmatched by any other hitter in 2026. This season represented the long-awaited regular-season masterpiece to complement his collection of iconic postseason moments. And as he stepped in against Kay, Alvarez looked primed to add another.

Not this time. Even after falling down 3-0, Kay executed a perfect fastball on the outer half to nab strike one looking. On the next pitch — another fastball away — Alvarez connected cleanly but lined out to left fielder Sam Antonacci for a gigantic second out.

Up came Isaac Paredes , a crucial cog behind Alvarez in the lineup, also capable of tying the game or seizing the lead with one swing. The threat Paredes posed proved substantial; he walked on four straight pitches, none near the strike zone. That loaded the bases for Altuve, who three innings earlier had smashed his 28th career postseason home run , putting him just one behind Manny Ramirez on the all-time leaderboard.

Altuve has been supplying seismic swings to the delight of the Houston home crowd for years. Even as his regular-season output has declined, more magic has always seemed to await in the playoffs. So here he was again, at the plate in the postseason for the 491st time, more than all but four hitters in MLB history. Surely he had another moment in him, one more run-scoring swing that could keep Houston's season alive for another day.

Nope. Altuve watched a sinker from Kay right down the middle for strike one, then swung at a changeup and lofted a harmless fly ball to right fielder Braden Montgomery for the third out, stranding the bases loaded and leaving the Astros trailing by one.

All year, Houston's slug-happy lineup led by a game-changer in Alvarez and a handful of accomplished hitters beyond him had been able to compensate for its shoddy run prevention. This lopsided recipe was good enough to win a historically weak AL West . But this week against the White Sox, it fell considerably short. After Altuve's flyout in the fifth, Houston mustered one baserunner over the remaining four innings.

Once that Astros rally was squashed, the White Sox could start to taste their first postseason series victory in more than two decades. Not since 2005 had this franchise popped bottles after advancing in the playoffs, and that year featured no shortage of champagne celebrations. A dominant run through October ended with a World Series title, won against these same Astros in Houston.

But now it's time for a new generation of ballplayers to make some postseason memories for the South Siders. And in the top of the sixth inning, second baseman Chase Meidroth put the finishing touches on Chicago's two-game sweep. Facing Astros reliever Bryan Abreu with two runners on, Meidroth torched a hanging 3-1 slider over the high wall in left-center field for a three-run homer and a 7-3 Sox lead, a score that would hold to the finish.

This defeat — the end of the line for this uninspiring iteration of the Astros — marked Houston's ninth consecutive postseason loss at Daikin (formerly Minute Maid) Park. The franchise's most recent home triumph came in Game 1 of the 2023 ALDS against Minnesota . Since Kyle Tucker caught the final out of Game 6 to win the 2022 World Series in Houston, the Astros have watched three different teams celebrate postseason series victories on their turf: the Rangers in the 2023 ALCS, the Tigers in the 2024 wild-card series and now the White Sox in 2026.

For Houston, the World Series window that Altuve and Alvarez have propped up for so long appears to finally be closing after a decade of dominance and excellence atop the American League.

And the White Sox, having improbably catapulted from the depths of a rebuild into contention, might just be entering an exciting new era for the franchise. They'll head to Cleveland to take on the AL Central rival Guardians in the ALDS starting Saturday.

articles.title: Red Sox Have Shrunk Back to Yankees' Little Brother After Embarrassing AL Wild Card Blowout
articles.summary: In the end, the second straight showdown between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series wasn't much of a show. It was more like watching a man trying to catch a falling redwood with his bare hands.
articles.body:
In the end, the second straight showdown between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series wasn't much of a show. It was more like watching a man trying to catch a falling redwood with his bare hands.

The Yankees were the redwood. The Red Sox were the man. The redwood won.

The shape of the Red Sox's splatter is that of a 2-0 sweep and an 18-2 run differential. No moral victory can be found in the wreckage. The Red Sox threw everything they had at the Yankees and they just kept coming, out-hitting, out-pitching and out-fielding their long-standing rivals with relative ease.

Those of us who have been around for long enough recognize this for what it is. This is what the Yankees-Red Sox rivalry used to feel like. The battles always felt big, but always had the same outcome: Yankees win and Red Sox lose, often in an embarrassing fashion. It was The Dark Times for Boston.

Well, that's now four straight losses with a total of five runs in playoff games against the Yankees. The Dark Times, it seems, have returned for the Red Sox.

The Red Sox Must Be Called Out for Having Done This To Themselves

One sympathizes with younger people who are very confused by all this.

Between 2002 and 2018, these were the two winningest teams in baseball. The Red Sox earned bragging rights because they tended to come out ahead in October. In those years, they won four World Series to the Yankees' one. The Red Sox also won nine of 10 head-to-head playoff matchups between Game 4 of the 2004 ALCS and Game 1 of the 2025 Wild Card Series.

Yeah, all that happened. That's why it's so jarring that this fair fight has so quickly turned into a rigged Mortal Kombat match. Or at least, it would be if there wasn't such an obvious culprit for the Red Sox's descent into mediocrity.

Nominally, John Henry still leads the same ownership group that has controlled the Red Sox since 2002. Realistically, they're one part of a multinational portfolio consisting of other sports franchises and enterprises. Private equity is also involved, because what else would you expect to hear in 2026?

The bottom line is hard to miss. In the 2000s and 2010s, the Red Sox routinely had a top-five payroll , even peaking at No. 1 in 2018 and 2019. Not anymore. They haven't had a top-five payroll even once in the 2020s and have indeed opened outside the top 10 in each of the last four years, including No. 12 this season.

Whatever this is, it's not maximum effort. Now more than ever, you can feel it.

The Red Sox Can Fix This…If They Want To

Granted, the Yankees don't spend or try as hard as they used to either. Yet they still throw their weight around more than the Red Sox, at least in that they still do the annual top-five payroll thing.

It matters. Since 2018, the Red Sox haven't finished ahead of the Yankees or won the AL East even once. For all their issues, the Yankees will take the bragging rights of having won the AL East three times in this span.

If you're a Red Sox fan looking for hope, it might be hard to see past how even the playoff teams of the last two years won just 89 and 87 games, respectively. The high-floor, low-ceiling vibes are strong, and compounded by the sheer flukiness of this year's playoff run. The Red Sox went 32-5 between June 25 and August 7. Everything on either side of that was forgettable or worse.

And yet, there are also this year's team WAR rankings:

Hey, look. The Red Sox were actually elite. And that was even without much from Garrett Crochet and Roman Anthony , who were meant to be the pillars of Boston's pitching and hitting this year. Injuries felled both of them.

They'll be back in 2027, and ditto for Willson Contreras , Wilyer Abreu , Ceddanne Rafaela , Payton Tolle , Ranger Suárez and pretty much every big name save for Sonny Gray , who could become a free agent if he doesn't retire. When you have a core like this, and you know that Franklin Arias , MLB's No. 2 prospect , is also coming, there's only one thing to do:

Henry must stop pinching pennies and tell Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow to go get the missing piece. As Boston finished fifth from the bottom of MLB in home runs, they need a slugger. The more dynamic, the better.

Randy Arozarena will be a free agent this winter. Better options could be available on the trade market, perhaps including Elly De La Cruz and Yordan Alvarez at the high end. Heck, Bobby Witt Jr.'s name even came up at one point this summer.

Given how the Red Sox have operated for most of the last decade, this feels like an allusion to the impossible. It's ultimately on Henry to push the envelope, and his pushing muscles haven't had a workout in a while.

If anything can spur him, it should be the return of The Dark Times. Because if he got the Red Sox out of those times just to lead them right back in, what was the point?

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Sonny Gray Calls Himself Best AL Pitcher, Questions Red Sox Future After Playoff Loss to Yankees
articles.summary: Boston Red Sox starting pitcher Sonny Gray wondered why he was removed during the team's 9-2 loss to the New York Yankees in Game 2 of their Wild Card Series clash on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Boston Red Sox starting pitcher Sonny Gray wondered why he was removed during the team's 9-2 loss to the New York Yankees in Game 2 of their Wild Card Series clash on Wednesday.

"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League the third time through the order," Gray said after the contest, per CBS Sports' Julian McWilliams . "I think that's a fact. I would have liked to be trusted in that moment."

He added that he felt "strong," "confident," and "convicted" before he was taken out.

With the defeat, the Red Sox were eliminated from the postseason.

Gray, who has a $30 million mutual option for his 2027 campaign, was also noncommittal about his future in Boston.

Gray pitched the first four innings for the Red Sox on Wednesday until he was removed with two outs and runners at the corners in the bottom of the fifth. He had only thrown 70 pitches at the time, while the Yankees led Boston 1-0.

Red Sox reliever Erik Miller wasn't able to keep New York from extending the lead after Gray's exit, as he gave up a single to Cody Bellinger that gave the Yankees a 2-0 edge.

New York's lineup continued to excel against Boston's bullpen, scoring seven runs over the next two innings to wrap up the lopsided win.

Gray was a key piece of the Red Sox rotation throughout the regular season, owning an 18-5 record in 29 starts to go along with a 2.72 ERA.

He was particularly sharp during the third time through the order, owning a 1.99 ERA and limiting opposing hitters to a .180/.235/.280 slash line in such situations (via FanGraphs ).

Gray didn't receive an opportunity to close out the fifth inning on Wednesday night, though.

articles.title: White Sox owner Jerry Reinsdorf jokes he may convert to Catholicism after playoff series win, letter from the Pope
articles.summary: The White Sox secured their first playoff series win since 2005 on Wednesday night in Houston.
articles.body:
The Catholic Church may have a new member after Wednesday night.

Chicago White Sox owner Jerry Reinsdorf, shortly after the franchise won their first playoff series since 2005, couldn't help but think about the letter he received from the Pope earlier this week.

"Imagine a Jewish kid from Brooklyn getting a letter from the Pope," he said, via ESPN's Jesse Rogers .

"I'm going to convert," he added, joking.

Hours before the White Sox's playoff opener against the Houston Astros on Tuesday, the club announced they had received a letter from Pope Leo XIV. The Pope is a Chicago native and undoubtedly the franchise's most famous fan.

The letter didn't specifically address the playoffs, but it was addressed to Reinsdorf and thanked him for a letter he had sent the Pope the previous month.

"It is my hope that the White Sox will continue to foster bonds of friendship and solidarity among people, and thus bear hopeful witness to the possibility of living and working together in peace," the Pope, previously known as Robert Prevost, wrote, in part .

While not specifically a "good luck in the playoffs" letter, it's easy to see why Reinsdorf feels the way he does about it.

The White Sox rolled to a 7-3 win over the Astros at Daikin Park on Wednesday night, which completed the sweep in their wild-card series. The White Sox never trailed throughout the two-game series, either.

The series win was the team's first since the 2005 season, when the White Sox won the World Series. This is their first trip to the American League Division Series since 2021, too, and comes on the heels of three straight 100-plus loss seasons.

The White Sox will take on the Cleveland Guardians in the ALDS starting on Saturday.

And though he may not be attending mass anytime soon, Reinsdorf and the White Sox are absolutely feeling the support from Vatican City.

The Brewers might be MLB's best team since March, record-wise, but San Diego is suddenly looking like a complete team playing with urgency. That turn of events has ended the Cubs' season more quickly than anyone might have expected. Chicago spent months in the NL's top wild-card spot, but it wound up being the Padres hosting the Cubs in a very loud stadium. It's an anticlimactic ending for a talented team, but that will happen in the playoffs.

articles.title: The New York Yankees did not need Aaron Judge to sweep the Red Sox
articles.summary: Max Fried, Cody Bellinger and Co. got it done in the wild-card round, leaving little doubt about which is the better team.
articles.body:
NEW YORK — For about 10 minutes, there was a ballgame.

The window opened around 9:56 p.m. ET on Wednesday. Boston first baseman Willson Contreras sliced a Max Fried fastball through the crisp Bronx air into the first row in right for a solo home run. That cut New York's lead in half. For the first time in this best-of-three wild-card series between longtime rivals, a Red Sox hitter touched home plate . And so, a glimmer of hope flickered in the visiting dugout as Game 2 flipped to the bottom of the sixth.

By 10:06 p.m., when rookie George Lombard Jr. laced an RBI single over the second baseman's head, that flame had already begun to falter. By the end of the inning, it was thoroughly extinguished.

Ten Yankees hitters came to the plate in the bottom of the sixth; six scored. Last year's AL Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet , injured for nearly the entire regular season, entered as a reliever and did not record an out (though he did strike out a batter). Boston's most trusted setup man, Garrett Whitlock , then entered the ballgame to serve up the final blow: a moon-scraping, three-run homer via Cody Bellinger that pushed New York's lead to seven .

Yankee Stadium rumbled as Bellinger's ball returned to Earth. Libations sprung into the sky like a Bellagio fountain of booze. Popcorn rained from the heavens. Bellinger rounded the sacks and entered the dugout to a tunnel of high-fives and atta-boys. The rest of this lopsided laugher was merely epilogue. By the ninth inning, Yankee fans were serenading the defeated Sox with "na, na, na, na, hey, hey, hey, goodbye." A few minutes later, they were hollering Sinatra's "New York, New York" as the Yankees strolled onto the diamond in a casual celebration.

No doubt — not a crumb — was left as to which is the better team.

"Total domination," a Yankees employee could be heard saying to a colleague in the champagne-soaked afterparty.

Predictably, New York skipper Aaron Boone offered Boston its flowers, but it was incredibly telling that the first question asked to him at his postgame media conference was: "Were you surprised by the margins of victory?"

"Yes," Boone, ever the politician, replied. "As I said, kind of all year, but even going into this series, that was a scary team to us, especially as well as they pitch. So for us to have the offensive outbreaks that we had here these last two nights and late, credit to those guys."

No more than 30 minutes later, Boone could be seen stampeding past the Yankees' clubhouse with neither a shirt nor a worry in the world. Nothing about this wild-card matchup provided any reason for him or any other Yankees employee to view the Red Sox as a scary team. No, this was a drubbing.

The Yankees outscored the Red Sox 18-2 across the two games. Boston mustered seven total hits, the fewest ever in a wild-card series (this format was implemented in 2022). It was a damning, telling offensive performance by a lineup that lacked both the impact and the depth of a legitimate championship contender. And while the Sox certainly felt the absence of Roman Anthony — the young slugger was scratched from the roster after suffering a wrist injury in Game 1 — not even a resuscitated, cryogenically unfrozen Ted Williams could've helped this Boston ballclub.

"You're thinking we're going to play closer games," Red Sox manager Chad Tracy admitted postgame. "They swung the bats extremely well. You've got to give them credit. It was frustrating."

Also frustrating, for Tracy, must have been the noticeable chasm in talent between the two clubs. The Red Sox drew deserved plaudits ahead of the series for their run-prevention prowess. And yet, on paper, the Yankees' rotation looked far more dangerous. And that's how it played out, with soon-to-be Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler dicing in Game 1 and Fried cruising in Game 2.

New York's decision to roster just 10 pitchers for this series was also an indication of the organization's immense level of confidence in its staff, particularly its starters. Why enter the battle with an army when a small special-ops unit can do the job?

"That's been the biggest strength for us throughout the year," Boone said of his team's rotation. "It sustained us. It got us through some difficult times. And I feel like they're all in a good place right now."

The Yankees' lineup is also clearly in a very good place. With captain Aaron Judge off the roster and watching from the dugout in a hoodie, New York's offense impressed. In both games, the Bombers needed a few innings to get revved up but eventually bludgeoned Boston's bullpen into submission. They tallied 26 total hits, the most by the Yanks in a two-game playoff span since 2004.

Judge's status for the ALDS against Tampa Bay remains a mystery. Fellow injured large man Giancarlo Stanton was on the roster for the wild-card round but wasn't called upon for a plate appearance. The Rays will likely present a stiffer challenge than whatever this was, but New York's lineup is humming at the perfect time.

Boston, meanwhile, didn't even get to play October baseball. When closer David Bednar punched out Caleb Durbin to conclude the proceedings, the clock read 11:14 p.m. ET.

September lived on. The Red Sox did not.

articles.title: New York Yankees Receive Bold Aaron Judge Prediction Amid MLB Playoffs Run
articles.summary: The New York Yankees are hoping to advance to the ALDS (obviously) and return the services of star outfielder Aaron Judge. Judge was left off the Yankees’ Wi...
articles.body:
The New York Yankees are hoping to advance to the ALDS (obviously) and return the services of star outfielder Aaron Judge .

Judge was left off the Yankees' Wild Card roster against the Red Sox as he continues to battle a calf injury.

If the Yankees are to advance, it's possible that Aaron Judge will return to the roster, but how long will he last?

In a recent bold prediction, FanSided.com believes that if Judge is activated to the Yankees playoff roster, it will be a short-lived move.

In a recent piece for FanSided.com, the contributors came up with 30 bold predictions, and one of them involved Aaron Judge, per Chris Landers:

Here is the headline for the cryptic prediction:

"Aaron Judge forces his way onto the Yankees roster — but doesn't last more than a game"

"This just has disaster written all over it. Judge suffered a Grade 2 calf strain on Sept. 16; less than two weeks later, he's publicly turning up the heat on his own team to let him on the Wild Card roster anyway. I doubt New York says no to its foundational star. I also doubt Judge is ready to be an impactful player."

Landers does have a point: if Judge does return, and he even swings the wrong way, his status could be in jeopardy.

It certainly would be something if the Yankees are able to advance to the Fall Classic without their megastar in Judge, which at this particular junction, feels entirely possible.

articles.title: Astros news: Joe Espada gives flowers to 'our franchise' Jose Altuve
articles.summary: The Houston Astros entered the playoffs with the worst record from a division winner in MLB history. Houston failed to clinch a winning record in the regular...
articles.body:
The Houston Astros entered the playoffs with the worst record from a division winner in MLB history. Houston failed to clinch a winning record in the regular season. But they had a chance to make right with a postseason upset over the Chicago White Sox .

This did not come to pass. The White Sox eliminated the Astros on Wednesday , defeating Houston in a two-game sweep. After the game, Astros manager Joe Espada was reflective, expressing his respect for franchise icon Jose Altuve .

"He is our franchise. You expected him to do something special in a game like today. He always finds ways to get our crowd going, get our team going. Just watching him play for so many years, it's incredible. I admire how he goes about it," Espada said, via MLB Network.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

The White Sox raced out to a 4-0 lead in this game. However, Houston didn't go away quietly. The Astros fought back and eventually came within one run in the fourth inning. Altuve hit a home run to make it a 4-3 game in that frame.

Houston was not able to claw all the way back, though. The White Sox added three runs off the bat of Chase Meidroth in the seventh inning. That home run was the decisive blow, sending the White Sox to the ALDS.

Espada's future with the Astros is in doubt. Houston has had a long track record of success in the American League. They won the World Series in 2017 and 2022 while being a regular participant in the ALCS. Now, the team is on the decline, and a shakeup in the dugout is possible.

articles.title: Red Sox veterans Sonny Gray and Willson Contreras speak out about team's decision-making after elimination by Yankees
articles.summary: The Red Sox players don't seem too happy with the club's leadership right now.
articles.body:
The Boston Red Sox were eliminated from the MLB playoffs on Wednesday . Two of their players had some notes for team leadership on their way out.

Both starting pitcher Sonny Gray and All-Star first baseman Willson Conteras clearly signaled disagreement with some part of the team's decision-making in the hours after their Game 2 loss to the New York Yankees . The Yankees swept the Red Sox, by an aggregate score of 18-2.

Game 2 hinged most on the decision to remove Gray in the fifth inning. Gray had been solid up to that point, allowing the game's only run on a solo homer by Luis García Jr. , but got into a jam with runners on the corners and two outs. Rather than leave Gray in to face left-hander Cody Bellinger , Red Sox manager Chad Tracy removed him for left-handed reliever Erik Miller . Gray was at 70 pitches.

The decision did not pay off, as Miller allowed a single to Bellinger that drove in a run, then another single to García, which was bailed out by an aggressive Yankees send resulting in an out at the plate.

The real damage arrived an inning later when Boston turned to ace Garrett Crochet , making his first appearance since April after an injured list stint due to shoulder and lat issues. Crochet failed to get an out, then the game got broken open when Tracy subbed in Garrett Whitlock .

It was an ugly loss, and it got even uglier when Gray openly questioned the decision to pull him :

"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that's a fact. I would have liked to live or die with with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. You can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way. I felt strong. I felt confident. I felt convicted.

Gray clearly believes the Red Sox were worried about the much-dreaded third-time-through-the-order penalty, which guides many teams' thinking during the postseason into counter-intuitive territory. To his point, that factor didn't appear to affect him much this season, as he held batters to a .180/.235/.280 slash line in his third time facing them this year.

There's also the matter of left/right splits. Gray has been better against left-handed batters than right-handed batters this season. Bellinger has been better against left-handed pitchers than right-handed pitchers this season.

Miller had better stats against lefties, but it could be argued there was little improvement for the Red Sox going with him over Gray. Tracy said after the game he was aware of Bellinger's reverse splits, but emphasized his confidence in his bullpen :

"With [Garrett] Crochet, [Garrett Whitlock] and [ Aroldis Chapman ] towards the back end there, and they were able to string a bunch of hits and we couldn't stop the bleeding there," he said. "It was pretty obvious that we were going to be aggressive in using that group. Like I said, they swung the bats. Didn't work out."

Contreras was also asked about the decision to pull Gray. His only response was to pretend to zip his mouth closed, clearly signaling disagreement.

Of course, the veteran had no problem telling reporters he was unhappy about the team's data-driven approach this year under chief baseball officer Craig Breslow :

"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball. The data is here to help us but at the end of the day, you're going to need experience and veteran guys to win games. There's a lot of stuff that I would like to say, but I'll state it like that."

Question: "You guys for much of the season, especially during the hot stretch, found so many fitting parts in the lineup. What do you think happened down the stretch and into the playoffs?" Contreras: "That's a good question. I'm not going to answer it because I don't want to give my honest answer. We got eliminated, that's the bottom line."

Question: "You guys for much of the season, especially during the hot stretch, found so many fitting parts in the lineup. What do you think happened down the stretch and into the playoffs?"

Contreras: "That's a good question. I'm not going to answer it because I don't want to give my honest answer. We got eliminated, that's the bottom line."

None of this is stuff you see in a harmonious organization, even after a playoff elimination. This is also far from the first time we've received signals that the players are unhappy with Breslow's guidance, as several spoke about the decision to fire manager Alex Cora in April and there was also Rafael Devers' infamous feud with the front office .

Ultimately, leadership comes down to results, and that's not exactly an argument in Breslow's favor. He took over for the fired Chaim Bloom in 2023 and the team has failed to win either 90 games or a playoff series in the three seasons since.

articles.title: Old men and the seams: Two moguls take their cuts at the knuckleball
articles.summary: A Korean video game mogul and a Brooklyn real estate investor both chased knuckleball dreams that collided over dinner in New York's Koreatown.
articles.body: In the summer of 2012 — when knuckleballer R. A. Dickey came out of nowhere to win the Cy Young award — I discovered my sons in our backyard teaching themselves the pitch. The knuck, a slow trick pitch that doesn’t spin, has a storied history of elevating longshots, retreads and dreamers to the major leagues — even the Hall of Fame. I resolved to see how far my kids could go. On the decade-long odyssey that followed, I learned that not only baseball-crazy boys harbored knuckleball dreams. Two wealthy business moguls did too. Their intersecting lives are one of the strange but true stories in my new book, "School of Hard Knucks: My Three Sons and Baseball’s Wildest Pitch." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Brooklyn real estate investor Howard Rich, a free-market guy who founded Americans for Limited Government, had Mets season tickets six rows behind home plate — the ideal place to watch Dickey’s knuckleball baffle hitters in 2012. "If the knuckleball’s so hard to hit," Rich ’ s wife Andrea asked one game, "why does only one pitcher throw it in the major leagues?" Great question, Rich thought. This was a market failure. He’d fix it by opening a school — the International Knuckleball Academy (IKA). He hired two minor league knucklers, Chris Nowlin and Zach Staniewicz to run it. On the other side of the globe, a 36-year-old South Korean who made a fortune in video games had never given up on his boyhood dream of playing pro baseball. "I thought if I could master the knuckleball," Min Hur told me, "I might still have a chance." Hur converted the roof of his Seoul office building into a personal training facility, with a retractable dome and cutting-edge pitch tracking technology. He’d also reached out to the greatest knuckleballer of all, Phil Niekro. "Phil invited me to his home in Atlanta and over a month taught me everything from the grip to the philosophy behind the pitch. He became my great mentor." Hur worked with another knuckleball legend, Charlie Hough, too. "He could take the spin off the ball pretty darn well," Hough recalled. In 2013, Hur hired a well-connected agent who got him tryouts with the Rangers, Mariners, and Diamondbacks. They all passed on Hur. Then the Rockland Boulders, an independent minor league team in upstate New York, agreed to give him a look. Min’s chauffeur drove him and his translator up from Manhattan every day of tryouts. He made the team and stepped away from his businesses to focus on his knuckleball career. The Boulders promoted Hur’s pro debut as" Min-Sanity," playing off the NBA’s "Lin-Sanity" craze when point guard Jeremy Lin caught fire with the Knicks. Min bussed up spectators from New York’s Korean neighborhoods and flew his family in from Seoul. They watched him pitch three innings and surrender five runs on five hits and four walks. He also hit three batters. Howard Rich read all about it, and wondered if Hur would want to partner with the IKA. He called Nowlin. " There’s a Korean billionaire in New York right now, and he loves knuckleballs," said Rich. "Set up a meting for us." Rich, Hur, Nowlin, and Staniewicz had dinner in Koreatown, but much was lost in translation. Hur remembers talking about knuckleballs, but nothing about an academy. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Rich forged ahead with the IKA, renting Dodgertown, the one-time spring training complex of the Los Angeles Dodgers. Staniewicz worried. "It’s hard enough to find people who want to throw the knuckleball, much less pay thousands of dollars a week to try to learn it," he told me. "That cut the pool of possible clients from, like, ten to two." Rich offered a financing plan. He told me about it last year when he took me to a Mets game. "I hired a hot-shot attorney to draft a contract so players could come for free, but if any went on to throw, say, ten pitches in the majors, we'd get a small percentage of their pay." Even still, the International Knuckleball Academy shut its doors before a single aspiring knuckler walked through them. Min Hur is still at it. I recently met him at a batting cage in Lower Manhattan. He’d flown in from Australia after a stint with the Melbourne Aces and was rendezvousing with a knuckleball coach from Buffalo named Joe Gannon. Hur’s now 50 years old. That’s ancient for most baseball players, but not too old for a knuckleballer. So the dream lives on. articles.title: Ranking Cubs SP Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: The Chicago Cubs will face some interesting decisions this offseason regarding their starting rotation.
articles.body:
The Chicago Cubs will face some interesting decisions this offseason regarding their starting rotation.

At the forefront of that will be veterans Kevin Gausman and Shota Imanaga, who are set to become free agents.

Gausman, 35, mostly struggled after being acquired from the Toronto Blue Jays.

Meanwhile, Imanaga made 30-plus starts for the first time in his career after accepting the qualifying offer last offseason. However, his fifth-place finish in 2024 NL Cy Young voting increasingly feels like an outlier.

The Cubs could let both Gausman and Imanaga, who will turn 34 in September 2027, leave in free agency. Justin Steele has barely pitched the last two seasons, Edward Cabrera had a disappointing first season in Chicago, and Matthew Boyd could also wind up a free agent if either side declines their half of a $15 million mutual option. So there's a lot to work through on the north side.

With all that acknowledged, here are five potential landing spots in free agency for Gausman and Imanaga.

Zac Gallen will likely depart in free agency after posting a 6.12 ERA across 104.1 innings during his eighth season with the Snakes. That could open the door for Gausman to sign a one-year deal and help stabilize the rotation.

Even the returning starters the Diamondbacks will have in 2027—Corbin Burnes, Eduardo Rodríguez, and Merrill Kelly—have notable injuries and/or underperformance in the not-so-distant past.

With Michael Soroka set to join Gallen in free agency, the D-Backs would be wise to add another veteran arm to their rotation. They might end up with a surplus heading into the season, but most teams end up needing far more than five starters to get through the year.

Gausman spent the final half of the season with the Cubs, but given how popular he was during his four-and-a-half seasons with the Blue Jays, it's not hard to imagine a Merrill Kelly-esque return this offseason for the veteran righty.

Max Scherzer, Jameson Taillon and Shane Bieber will be coming off the books this offseason. Bowden Francis had Tommy John surgery in February, so it might be a stretch for him to be ready for Opening Day. José Berríos had Tommy John surgery in May, so he's more likely in play for the second half of the 2027 season. Cody Ponce will also be returning from a major procedure, as he tore the ACL in his right knee in April.

The point is, the Blue Jays will need starting pitching depth heading into 2027. A one-year deal with Gausman would give them that, even if he's no longer a top-of-the-rotation starter.

In each of the past two offseasons, San Francisco president of baseball operations Buster Posey has given a one-year deal to a veteran righty; Justin Verlander in 2025 and Tyler Mahle in 2026.

Could Gausman be that guy in 2027? Even if we assume the Giants will keep resisting Logan Webb trade inquiries, they could still add another veteran to Tiny Vitello's rotation after trading both Mahle and Robbie Ray before the trade deadline.

Gausman, of course, previously pitched for the Giants. He really hit his stride during his two seasons with the Giants in 2020 and 2021, going 17-9 with a 3.00 ERA over 251.2 innings.

Cubs 2026 Offseason Guide After Wild Card Loss

As CJ Abrams and James Wood get more expensive, it's unclear how the Nationals will operate this offseason. Will they spend money to build around what was one of baseball's better offenses for most of the year, or will they seriously consider trade offers for one or both of their lineup anchors?

Either way, the Nats will need innings from their rotation. Gausman has six consecutive seasons of at least 170 innings pitched, so at the very least, he's a good bet to eat innings for them. He also has a higher ceiling than Miles Mikolas, whom Washington signed hoping for a career revival before the 2026 season.

The Nationals just gave Cade Cavalli a contract extension, but to really compete, they need to add a bunch of pitching to both the starting rotation and the bullpen. Gausman could give them a much-needed veteran presence.

Prior to the trade deadline, the Tigers dealt both Tarik Skubal and Casey Mize. Verlander—who hardly pitched at all in his final season—will be retiring. It's safe to say that president of baseball operations Scott Harris will be in the market for starting pitching this offseason.

While Skubal has publicly said he would consider a return to the Tigers in free agency, it's hard to imagine owner Christopher Ilitch authorizing Harris to sign a deal exceeding Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million pact.

Gausman would be a more affordable option, slotting into a rotation also set to feature Framber Valdez, Keider Montero and Jackson Jobe in 2027.

Given the uncertainty in the Cubs' rotation, one would think they'd at least keep tabs on the market for Shota Imanaga in the offseason.

With that said, the Cubs declined a three-year, $57.75 million option on Imanaga's contract last offseason. Granted, they ultimately issued him the one-year, $22.025 million qualifying offer, but from the moment they declined that option, it felt like time was ticking on Imanaga's tenure with the Cubs.

The Cubs may have hoped Imanaga would decline their QO last offseason, setting them up to receive draft-pick compensation if he signed elsewhere. This time around, Jed Hoyer and company will be left empty-handed if Imanaga walks.

As mentioned with Gausman, the Nationals need veteran pitching. Take any starting pitcher that's a free agent—particularly ones who aren't likely to command gigantic contracts—and they probably will be an on-paper fit for the Nationals.

Perhaps they could circle back with Foster Griffin in free agency because he's struggled since being dealt to the Cleveland Guardians. If not, Imanaga could make sense.

Unlike with Gausman, Imanaga could receive multiple years in free agency, so that's something to weigh when considering him.

The Cubs might not represent Imanaga's only opportunity to remain in Chicago this offseason.

With a lineup that includes Miguel Vargas, Chase Meidroth, Munetaka Murakami and Tristan Peters, there's a good young nucleus of offensive talent on the South Side. If you're wondering how the White Sox went from 121 losses in 2024 to the postseason two years later, that's a pretty good place to start.

Still, this team isn't a finished product. Sean Burke and Davis Martin are a nice one-two punch, but there's not necessarily a slam-dunk starting pitching prospect near the majors. So adding Imanaga could help the White Sox make a second consecutive postseason appearance in 2027.

As with Gausman, the Giants could make some sense for Imanaga. He would replace the left-handed presence they lost when trading the aforementioned Ray to the San Diego Padres.

Imanaga has a 4.15 ERA over two career starts at Oracle Park, but pitching his home games in such a pitcher-friendly environment could help him limit the number of home runs he allows.

If Logan Webb bounces back in 2027, some combination of him, Imanaga and Landen Roupp could be a pretty good start to a rotation. Posey and company might have to add multiple arms in free agency after moving Ray and Mahle before the trade deadline.

Basically the entire Padres rotation will be free agents after this season. That might sound like hyperbole, but it's not.

Ray and Mize were acquired as rentals before the trade deadline. Walker Buehler, who logged over 150 innings, is a free agent. Michael King and Nick Pivetta can also opt out of their contracts and become free agents.

So essentially, every free-agent pitcher makes sense as a fit for the Padres. Imanaga—who has five shutout innings in his career at Petco Park—is among them.

articles.title: Cubs 2026 Offseason Guide on Free Agents, Trade Targets, More Roster Shakeups After Wild Card Loss
articles.summary: The Chicago Cubs had the highest-scoring offense in baseball in 2026 and were also the league's best defensive team by almost every measure, but that wasn't enough to keep them out of an early playoff exit.
articles.body:
The Chicago Cubs had the highest-scoring offense in baseball in 2026 and were also the league's best defensive team by almost every measure, but that wasn't enough to keep them out of an early playoff exit.

The offense was silenced in Game 1 when Padres ace Michael King carried a no-hitter into the seventh inning, and they fell behind early in Game 2 and couldn't claw back in another quiet night from their bats against Nick Pivetta and the San Diego bullpen.

The biggest immediate question will be whether they push to re-sign one or both of Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ, but the more pressing need will be to upgrade a pitching staff that was the team's clear weakness throughout the 2026 season.

Rebuilding the bullpen, upgrading the rotation and retooling the outfield are all part of the offseason to-do list, and we've addressed all of that and more in the Cubs' offseason guide.

OF Seiya Suzuki OF Ian Happ OF Michael Conforto OF Tyrone Taylor 1B Tyler Austin

Pete Crow-Armstrong will return to anchor the Cubs outfield from center field, but who will flank him in right and left field is still up in the air.

Seiya Suzuki, Ian Happ, Michael Conforto, and Tyrone Taylor accounted for 295 of the 324 starts at the corner outfield spots, with most of the remaining playing time going to Matt Shaw in his super-utility role, so there aren't many viable in-house replacement options.

Suzuki (131 OPS+, 26 HR, 5.1 WAR) would be extremely difficult to replace in the middle of the lineup, while Happ (103 OPS+, 24 HR, 2.9 WAR) is the team's longest-tenured player and a veteran leader.

The club will likely try to re-sign one of them, but both might be a stretch. A reunion with Taylor, given how well he played in a platoon role against left-handed pitching, is also worth considering.

C Carson Kelly ($7.5 million mutual option)

A middling season from Miguel Amaya and the trade of Moisés Ballesteros leave the Cubs without an obvious replacement behind the plate if Kelly walks after starting 94 games behind the dish in 2026.

The 32-year-old has been a good fit for the Cubs, and while he'll likely decline his end of the mutual option, a quick re-up on a new multi-year deal would make sense for both sides.

SP Shota Imanaga SP Kevin Gausman SP David Peterson RP Aaron Civale

Shota Imanaga was the Cubs' best starter this season, finishing 11-10 with a 3.77 ERA, 1.10 WHIP and 174 strikeouts in 174.1 innings. He remained homer-prone, serving up 35 long balls, but finished on a high note with a 2.25 ERA over five September starts.

Kevin Gausman was a deadline rental, while David Peterson proved to be a great scrapheap pickup, posting a 3.70 ERA in 80.1 innings over 15 starts after the Mets cut him loose.

Veteran Aaron Civale posted a 1.72 ERA over 36.2 innings in 18 relief appearances, recording a pair of saves at the height of the club's bullpen uncertainty. He might prefer a chance to start elsewhere.

SP Matthew Boyd ($15 million mutual option) SP Clay Holmes ($12 million player option) RP Hunter Harvey ($8 million mutual option) SP/RP Colin Rea ($7.5 million club option) RP Caleb Thielbar ($6 million mutual option) RP Jacob Webb ($2.5 million club option)

Matthew Boyd and Clay Holmes are safe bets to test free agency, while Hunter Harvey will be a no-brainer to have his option declined and Caleb Thielbar will also likely be cut loose.

Colin Rea (34 G, 19 GS, 4.34 ERA, 137.0 IP) was a valuable swingman, finishing second on the club in innings pitched, and $7.5 million is a reasonable price tag for what he provides.

The easy decision here is to exercise Jacob Webb's reasonable club option, as he recorded a team-high nine saves while posting a 3.36 ERA and 9.8 K/9 in 68 appearances.

Starting Pitching: The Cubs will essentially be rebuilding their rotation from the ground up, assuming Shota Imanaga, Matthew Boyd, Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes all hit the open market. A healthy Justin Steele should be ready to return to the starting staff, while Edward Cabrera will be given every chance to reclaim his spot in the rotation, but this is a complete teardown-and-rebuild situation.

Relief Pitching: A healthy Daniel Palencia, deadline pickup Ryan Zeferjahn, breakout lefty Ryan Rolison and veteran Jacob Webb give the Cubs some pieces to build around in the bullpen, but they need multiple established veterans to fill in the gaps around them.

Outfielder: Unless they simply re-up with Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ, which seems unlikely given their expected cost and the team's other needs, the outfield will look new in 2027. Former top prospect Kevin Alcantara could get an extended look this spring, and Matt Shaw could theoretically settle in as an everyday outfielder, but at least one notable outside addition is likely.

Potential Landing Spots for Cubs stars Kevin Gausman and Shota Imanaga

The Cubs should at least be in the Tarik Skubal conversation given their major-market status and clear need for a bona fide staff ace, but this is more than a one-piece-away situation.

Freddy Peralta and Trevor Rogers are the other frontline-caliber arms on the market this winter, while a reunion with Shota Imanaga , Clay Holmes or Kevin Gausman is a possibility. The next tier down will also be in play, with Tyler Mahle , Casey Mize , Nick Martinez , Foster Griffin , Jack Flaherty and Kris Bubic among the names to watch.

On the reliever side of things, Adrian Morejón , Alex Vesia and Bryan Abreu represent proven setup options with premium stuff, while more affordable options like Brock Burke , JoJo Romero and Jason Adam would also provide a boost. As for proven closers, David Bednar and Raisel Iglesias will be free agents, but a healthy Daniel Palencia is likely the ninth-inning guy.

To address the mass exodus in the outfield, expect a push to re-sign Seiya Suzuki or Ian Happ, and perhaps Tyrone Taylor or Michael Conforto if they are amenable to a part-time role.

Taylor Ward , Ramon Laureano and Adolis García are potential buy-low targets, but the trade market might be preferred to breaking the bank on top names like Randy Arozarena or Trent Grisham .

With a 3.73 ERA, 1.09 WHIP and 205 strikeouts in 186 innings, Gilbert would comfortably be the No. 2 starter on the market this offseason behind Tarik Skubal if he were a free agent.

Instead, he has one year of club control remaining, and after making just over $10 million in 2026, he will be less of a payroll drain than several second-tier free-agent options. The prospect price would be steep, but he would be an impact addition to plug their biggest roster hole.

Ryan is in the same free-agent class as Gilbert and was an All-Star for the second straight year in 2026, logging a 3.79 ERA, 1.16 WHIP, and 159 strikeouts in 144.2 innings. The Twins were hesitant to move him last winter, but if they finally lean into a rebuild, he's their top trade chip.

Ian Happ has won four straight NL Gold Glove awards in left field. What better way to replace him than with the guy who has won the AL Gold Glove at the same position every year over that same four-year stretch? The Cubs have enough thump to offset Kwan's lack of extra-base impact, and an elite defensive team would arguably get even better while adding a table-setting bat.

Starting Lineup C Carson Kelly 1B Michael Busch 2B Nico Hoerner 3B Alex Bregman SS Dansby Swanson LF Matt Shaw CF Pete Crow-Armstrong RF Seiya Suzuki DH Owen Ayers (R)

Bench C Miguel Amaya 1B/OF B.J. Murray IF James Triantos OF Kevin Alcantara

A reunion with Seiya Suzuki and a new multi-year deal for Carson Kelly would keep the Cubs' offensive core intact, and Matt Shaw deserves regular playing time in left field after logging a 102 OPS+ over 202 plate appearances in a utility role. They can scour the bargain bin in free agency to fill out the bench, but have plenty of MLB-ready options down on the farm.

Starting Rotation RHP Logan Gilbert LHP Justin Steele RHP Ben Brown RHP Nick Martinez LHP Kris Bubic

Bullpen RHP Javier Assad RHP Colin Rea RHP Jacob Webb LHP Brock Burke RHP Jason Adam LHP Ryan Rolison RHP Ryan Zeferjahn RHP Daniel Palencia

A blockbuster deal to acquire Logan Gilbert would give the Cubs enough financial flexibility to target a few mid-level arms like Nick Martinez and a healthy Kris Bubic, while Javier Assad and Colin Rea would provide rotation depth. Breaking the bank on a top-tier reliever might not be in the cards, but Brock Burke and Jason Adam can handle high-leverage work.

articles.title: Aaron Judge Says Knicks Inspired Yankees in Viral Video Celebrating Win vs. Red Sox in MLB Playoffs
articles.summary: After watching the New York Knicks bring an NBA championship to the city over the summer, the New York Yankees are trying to keep the good vibes going following their sweep of the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card series.
articles.body:
After watching the New York Knicks bring an NBA championship to the city over the summer, the New York Yankees are trying to keep the good vibes going following their sweep of the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card series.

Yankees star Aaron Judge told reporters during the locker room celebration after Wednesday's 9-2 victory over Boston they are taking inspiration from the Knicks' playoff run.

Judge's status for the ALDS is still up in the air after he missed the Red Sox series due to a calf injury.

The Yankees did have a Knicks-esque level of dominance in this series by outscoring the Red Sox 18-2 in the two games. The Knicks' average margin of victory of 14.9 points per game in the NBA playoffs was the second-highest mark ever.

Next up for the Yankees in their quest for a World Series title is an ALDS showdown with the Tampa Bay Rays. Game 1 will be played at Tropicana Field on Saturday at 6:30 p.m. ET.

articles.title: Garrett Crochet Feels 'Like S--t' and 'Little Bit at Fault' After Red Sox's Playoff Loss to Yankees
articles.summary: The Boston Red Sox attempt to utilize Garrett Crochet out of their bullpen for the playoffs after missing five months in the regular season backfired in Game 2 of the American League Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.
articles.body:
The Boston Red Sox attempt to utilize Garrett Crochet out of their bullpen for the playoffs after missing five months in the regular season backfired in Game 2 of the American League Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.

Crochet, who didn't record an out and was charged with four earned runs on Wednesday night, told reporters after the game he feels "like s--t"and a "little bit at fault" for the 9-2 loss.

Crochet last appeared in an MLB game on April 25 when he tossed six shutout innings in a 17-1 win over the Baltimore Orioles. He went on the injured list four days later due to shoulder inflammation .

Despite not having to undergo surgery, Crochet's recovery process was long and got extended in part because he suffered a lat strain in June.

When the Red Sox unveiled their wild-card roster, Crochet was included as an option for manager Chad Tracy to use out of the bullpen. He entered the game to start the bottom of the sixth inning with Boston trailing 2-1.

Crochet struck out Spencer Jones to start the frame, but a wild pitch allowed Jones to reach first base. The left-hander followed by giving up three straight singles and was pulled in favor of Garrett Whitlock, who allowed all three inherited runners to score.

The big blast in the inning was Cody Bellinger's three-run homer off Whitlock that made it 8-1 and all but ended any hope Boston had.

Crochet was put in a no-win situation and that's how it played out. This was a frustrating season for him coming off an incredible 2025 in which he finished second in AL Cy Young voting.

This is the second consecutive year the Red Sox's season has ended with a loss to the Yankees in the wild-card round.

articles.title: Aaron Judge hosted 232 young Bronx baseball players in August 2026; his ALL RISE Foundation also donated $9,999.99 to support Little League equipment
articles.summary: The Aaron Judge ALL RISE Foundation put 232 Bronx Little Leaguers on a Fordham University field on August 11, 2026, and the Yankees captain spent the day
articles.body: The Aaron Judge ALL RISE Foundation put 232 Bronx Little Leaguers on a Fordham University field on August 11, 2026, and the Yankees captain spent the day with them while still working his way back from injury. Judge ran a free Baseball ProCamp with former Yankee Tyler Wade, a program backed by Major League Baseball and the MLB Players Association. The kids came from nine neighborhood leagues, ran drills, raced by age group and posed for team photos.ALL RISE gave $9,999.99 to Bronx Little League programs for bats, baseballs and other gear, and the odd-looking figure was chosen on purpose. Judge also gave the group his answer on what matters most when you are learning the game. The camp is one piece of a foundation he started in 2018, and its tax filings show who has been paying for the rest.Aaron Judge's ALL RISE Foundation brings Baseball ProCamp to Bronx kidsThe camp ran on Tuesday, August 11, at Fordham University, free of charge and closed to the general public. The foundation says it was made possible by a grant from the MLB-MLBPA Youth Development Foundation, with ALL RISE working alongside Little League International, GSE Worldwide and ProCamps. Little League Urban Initiative helped coordinate who showed up from around the borough. The foundation's release, dated August 12 and posted on its site September 1, frames the day as a chance for kids to learn from a role model.Those 232 players belonged to nine Bronx programs: South Riverdale, Van Nest, Pelham Parkway, Pelham Bay, Parkchester, Jaws and Taino, Co-Op City, City Island and Castle Hill. Ten students from The Brotherhood Sister Sol, a local organization, joined them.Judge and Wade stayed on the field for the full day. They led drills, played games, ran races split by age group and traded stories from their own careers. Every team got a photo with the Yankees captain. The YES Network posted about the camp the same day, noting that Judge may still be working on his on-field return but has no shortage of action away from it.When asked which lesson from his early years mattered most, Judge told the players, "It's important to hustle, but the most important is to be a good teammate."The $9,999.99 donation came with its own logic. Judge wears No. 99, and the foundation says the Bronx has 99 Little League teams. The money is meant for baseballs, bats and other equipment for those programs. MLB.com and the foundation's own release agree on the amount and the reasoning.Each camper also left with a swag bag. The contents came from DICK'S Sporting Goods, Fanatics, the MLB Players Association, Conagra Brands/David Seeds, Big League Chew, Topps, Rawlings, Jordan Brand, ALL RISE and ProCamps, and included baseball merchandise and memorabilia.What does Aaron Judge's ALL RISE Foundation do?Judge founded ALL RISE in 2018 with a stated goal of building character in young people and steering them toward responsible citizenship. The foundation runs awards and incentive programs that reward academic improvement at schools and local groups, supports children and teens facing hard health or family circumstances, and holds fundraisers that feed its Mini-Grants and other programs. Its reach covers the Bronx, Fresno County and San Joaquin County in California.The list of programs goes well past baseball. It includes the Aspiring Leaders Initiative, a Linden High School scholarship, Bronx Educational All-Star Day, leadership master classes and a reading effort called ALL RISE to Read, plus the baseball camp itself. Its mission statement says it wants to engage kids in activities that help them reach their full potential.Public tax filings summarized by philanthropy.org show $435,000 across 21 grants from 15 funders between 2019 and 2024, according to philanthropy.org. Major League Baseball Charities is the largest, with $162,000 over three grants from 2022 to 2024. The Duane Davis Foundation gave $100,000 in two grants, and the Fanatics Charitable Foundation added $50,000 in 2024. Turn 2 Foundation and the McCormick Family Foundation each contributed $25,000, in 2022 and 2021.Aaron Judge turned Yankees experiences into ALL RISE Foundation auction bidsThe 9/9 for 99 auction gave Yankees fans a way to bid on time with Judge. It has hosted 1,205 kids at baseball camps and paid registration costs for educators, students and parents to attend Leadership Master Class webinars.One Mini-Grant recipient, the ACTS Foundation, told the outlet that ALL RISE support paid for weekly meals and classroom space. The money also sent two of its students to summer camp.Athlon traced the whole idea back to a mother, a mentor and a number Yankees fans know by heart. The format has continued into this season. On Friday, September 4, 2026, Athlon Sports reported that Judge launched another auction to raise funds, with seats to a Yankees home game and an autographed bat among the items. Judge, who has stayed active in funding the foundation, shared a link so fans could place bids, and he did it while still preparing for his own return to the lineup.What is Aaron Judge's net worth in 2026?Celebrity Net Worth puts Judge's net worth at $100 million. He then hit 62 home runs to break Roger Maris' American League record and won the first of three MVP awards. On December 7, 2022, he signed a nine-year, $360 million deal, which the site says brought him an extra $146.5 million in guaranteed money.By the end of the 2025 season, he had collected about $156 million in MLB salary and signing bonuses, including a $1.8 million bonus after the 2013 draft. Another $40 million is due in 2026, and the same figure runs through 2031. articles.title: Willson Contreras Shades Red Sox's Use of Analytics in Video After Sonny Gray's Early Exit
articles.summary: Willson Contreras indicated he felt overuse of analytics led Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy to pull Sonny Gray from Wednesday's Wild Card round elimination loss after just 70 pitches against the New York Yankees.
articles.body:
Willson Contreras indicated he felt overuse of analytics led Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy to pull Sonny Gray from Wednesday's Wild Card round elimination loss after just 70 pitches against the New York Yankees.

Contreras initially responded to reporters asking about his reaction to Gray's fifth-inning exit from the 9-2 loss by miming zipping his lips before elaborating.

"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that are telling you what to do, because this is baseball," Contreras said (h/t SNY). "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you're going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."

When asked if he felt the Red Sox relied too much on data, Contreras nodded as he said, "If you watch the game."

Tracy, who had also pulled Game 1 starter Payton Tolle early, called Gray off the mound with two runners on base, one out remaining and the Red Sox trailing by one run in the bottom of the fifth.

Gray was replaced by Erik Miller, who on his third pitch of the game allowed a two-RBI single from Cody Bellinger.

Tracy then turned to Garrett Crochet for the sixth inning. Crochet allowed a run and loaded the bases until he was removed for Garrett Whitlock, who allowed five more runs before he was able to close out the frame.

Tracy said after the elimination loss he used the same reasoning to pull Gray as he had to remove Tolle from a Game 1 shutout loss to the Yankees.

"We're trailing. We're struggling to score runs, and when you get into spots where you're struggling to score runs and you're already trailing, you feel like you've got to be aggressive," Tracy told reporters Wednesday night.

The Yankees will now advance to face the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS, while the Red Sox will concede their second Wild Card loss in as many years. Ranger Suárez, who was slated to start a potential deciding Game 3, will not pitch this postseason.

The Red Sox fired former manager Alex Cora and turned to Tracy following a 10-17 start to the season. Tracy lost his interim tag and inked a three-year extension after leading the club to clinch a postseason berth.

Tracy will now be tasked with helping his club find a way to respond next fall to scoring two runs across their two postseason games.
