Ranking Luis Arraez's Top Landing Spots Ahead of FA 🔢

The Dark Horse: San Diego Padres (+1000)

Consistently inconsistent, the Padres "earned" these odds with an up-down-season that saw them score just 41 more runs than their opponents. For context, the other three NL teams still standing all bettered their opponents by at least 116 runs.

Remember, though, the World Series doesn't always crown the campaign's best team. Sometimes a club catches fire down the stretch and rides the heat wave all the way to a title, and maybe the Padres are en route to doing exactly that. Including their Wild-Card sweep of the Chicago Cubs (which featured a 12-1 advantage in scoring), they've now won 19 of their last 22 games.

They have momentum-shifting stars in their lineup (Fernando Tatís Jr., Manny Machado and Jackson Merrill) and arguably the best closer in baseball (Mason Miller). If they can summon quantity and quality innings out of their rotation, they could be the latest team to prove that heating up at the right time sometimes delivers a championship parade.

articles.title: MLB Playoffs 2026 Divisional Round Picks and Predictions for Every Series
articles.summary: Welcome to the next round of the 2026 MLB playoffs. It's the Division Series. Eight teams will enter. Four will advance.
articles.body:
Welcome to the next round of the 2026 MLB playoffs. It's the Division Series. Eight teams will enter. Four will advance.

Even if it's not quite Thunderdome stakes, we're getting there as the calendar advances to the World Series. And the Division Series is where things get interesting. No more cushy series of all home games for the higher seeds. No more best-of-threes. These are best-of-five series featuring at least one plane ride.

On the American League side, there's nothing but well-worn division rivalries. The Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Guardians will decide, once and for all, who is the best of the AL Central. The New York Yankees and Tampa Bay Rays will do the same for the AL East.

On the National League side, we have a San Diego Padres vs. Milwaukee Brewers matchup that none of us knew we wanted until recently. And for the first time in five years, the Los Angeles Dodgers and Atlanta Braves are renewing an October rivalry that has had some heated moments.

Here's where the set-up stops and we get down to brass tacks. Time for some fresh predictions, both for all four Division Series and the rest of the 2026 postseason to come.

AL Division Series A: Chicago White Sox vs. Cleveland Guardians

Game 1: Saturday, October 3 in Cleveland at 1 p.m. ET

Game 2: Monday, October 5 in Cleveland at 5 p.m. ET

Game 3: Wednesday, October 7 in Chicago (Time TBD)

Game 4*: Thursday, October 8 in Chicago (Time TBD)

Game 5*: Saturday, October 10 in Cleveland (Time TBD)

Regular Season Series: White Sox 7-6 with +1 run differential

Matchup to Watch: Chicago's style of offense vs. Cleveland's style of offense

They really aren't the same, and you can tell by looking at how the two sides hit home runs during the regular season:

The White Sox unsurprisingly had the better overall offense of the two clubs, outscoring Cleveland by just about 100 total runs (i.e., 98). They overwhelmed Houston in the Wild Card Series despite hitting only two homers, which accounted for four of their 13 runs.

Cleveland pitchers may have to go into shutdown mode to keep this series winnable. To this end, it can only help that Gavin Williams and company had the AL's highest strikeout rate after the trade deadline.

This is the first year in what feels like forever that Ramírez was not one of the best players in baseball. He had a .688 OPS for the year, and a dismal .598 OPS in the second half.

The latter stretch coincides with J-Ram's return from a broken hamate, and he also battled some left wrist inflammation toward the end. If you're the Guardians, your hope is that the first-round bye did his body some good.

Remember that note about how Guardians pitchers struck guys out down the stretch? That could be the deciding factor in this series, as White Sox hitters tied for the league's fifth-highest strikeout rate.

Also, don't read too much into the White Sox's victory on the road in the Wild Card Series. Daikin Park was hardly a hostile environment .

The White Sox were 36-45 on the road this year. The Guardians were 41-40 at home. It's not quite check and mate, but it at least hints toward a solid bet.

AL Division Series B: New York Yankees vs. Tampa Bay Rays

Game 1: Saturday, October 3 in Tampa at 6:30 p.m. ET

Game 2: Monday, October 5 in Tampa at 8 p.m. ET

Game 3: Wednesday, October 7 in New York (Time TBD)

Game 4*: Thursday, October 8 in New York (Time TBD)

Game 5*: Saturday, October 10 in Tampa (Time TBD)

Regular Season Series: Rays 7-6 with -9 run differential

Matchup to Watch: The Rays vs. the sum of their parts

We know what the Yankees are all about. They hit a bunch of home runs, and they have at least two aces in Cam Schlittler and Max Fried. Maybe four, depending on your thoughts on the present-day versions of Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón.

What makes the Rays such a good team is more nebulous. Something went into them winning 98 games this year, and fingers can point toward such directions as good defense, lots of contact and aggressive baserunning. Honestly, they didn't do a whole lot poorly.

However, they also overachieved their expected record by eight wins. Nothing wrong with that in the regular season, but one is always wary of teams that exceed the sum of their parts come the postseason. That one Billy Beane quote from Moneyball is a meme for a reason , after all.

The Yankees did just fine without their three-time MVP in the Wild Card Series against Boston, which was merely the latest variation on long-running theme. They have been pretty much fine without him since June.

The question nonetheless lingers if the Yankees can really take off if Judge is able to suit up for them. To this end, the slugger has vowed to be back from a calf strain "as fast as I can."

Sorry, Rays. This is ultimately indicative of trust issues with your contention model. Because even if the Yankees haven't won a World Series since 2009, what they do has a general track record of success in October more generally.

Homers and whiffs. Whiffs and homers. No matter how you order them, the Yankees can do both. Just ask the Boston Red Sox, who felt the sting of four homers and 45 whiffs in just two games in the Wild Card Series.

NL Division Series A: Atlanta Braves vs. Los Angeles Dodgers

Game 1: Saturday, October 3 in Los Angeles at 4 p.m. ET

Game 2: Sunday, October 4 in Los Angeles at 8 p.m. ET

Game 3: Tuesday, October 6 in Atlanta (Time TBD)

Game 4*: Wednesday, October 7 in Atlanta (Time TBD)

Game 5*: Friday, October 9 in Los Angeles (Time TBD)

Regular Season Series: Braves 5-1 with +11 run differential

Matchup to Watch: Braves hitters vs. the Dodgers' stuff

The day after the regular season ended, Paul Hembekides of ESPN posted an interesting series of stats showing how the 12 playoff offenses did against pitchers with above-average stuff.

After the trade deadline, the Braves were the worst with an OPS of .619. In that same time span, Dodgers pitchers co-led the league with a Stuff+ score of 108.

The other team tied with the Dodgers was the Philadelphia Phillies, and the Braves obviously survived that matchup. Yet their offense didn't have the easiest time doing so, and the Phillies didn't throw Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto at them like the Dodgers will.

Where were you when Ohtani last homered? This is a harder question to answer than it usually is, as you have to go back to August 18 to find the last time the four-time MVP hit one over the fence.

That's how much nagging injuries slowed Ohtani down the stretch, so the Dodgers must be hoping the first-round bye gets him right. If so, he stands to build on a career .940 OPS in the playoffs.

The Braves had the Dodgers' number this season, including in a three-game sweep that happened relatively recently in late August. So, they have that going for them.

Even so, one of these teams just plain looks superior, and it's not the Braves. Their offense seems especially ripe for a dose of humble pie, as it came into the postseason having failed to reach a .700 OPS in three of the season's last four months.

NL Division Series B: San Diego Padres vs. Milwaukee Brewers

Game 1: Saturday, October 3 in Milwaukee at 8:30 p.m. ET

Game 2: Sunday, October 4 in Milwaukee at 4 p.m. ET

Game 3: Tuesday, October 6 in San Diego (Time TBD)

Game 4*: Wednesday, October 7 in San Diego (Time TBD)

Game 5*: Friday, October 9 in Milwaukee (Time TBD)

Regular Season Series: Padres 4-2 with +5 run differential

Matchup to Watch: The Padres vs. Jacob Misiorowski's heat

You don't just hit Misiorowski. He held opposing batters to a .157 average this season, the lowest in history for an ERA title qualifier.

He leans on his fastball 63.3 percent of the time. You would too if you averaged 100.6 mph. Which brings us to the irony of how hitters managed a .176 average against it. If given the choice, a hitter should want the heat over the secondary offerings that combined for a .136 average this season.

Unless, maybe, you're a Padres hitter. Nobody hits 100-plus mph well, but their .137 average against that kind of velocity was 21st in baseball.

It's the Brewers who have home-field advantage in this series, and the word "advantage" can't be overstated. They went 55-26 at American Family Field this season.

And yet, we all watched the Padres in the Wild Card Series. More to the point, we all heard how loud Petco Park was. Its crowd has been consistently boisterous for a while now, as San Diego is 28-6 in its last 34 home games.

The Brewers are the better overall team in this series, but that isn't going to translate into a romp. The Padres hit more home runs, for one thing. For another, the back end of their bullpen is just absurdly good.

Yet if this series goes the distance, Milwaukee will have two major advantages: three games at home and two starts by Misiorowski.

ALCS: New York Yankees over Cleveland Guardians in 5

So, the exact same result as when these two teams met in the ALCS in 2024. And would anyone really expect anything different if this is the matchup?

With or without Aaron Judge, the Yankees would pose an even bigger over-the-fence threat than the Guardians will have faced in the Division Series against Chicago. And whereas the White Sox don't have an ace, the Yankees again fall in the two-to-four range.

Heck, what's one more dunk on the Guardians? Back in 2024, even a darn near 40-40 José Ramírez couldn't swing things in Cleveland's favor in the ALCS. Barring some sort of time displacement, that guy doesn't seem likely to show up in 2026.

NLCS: Milwaukee Brewers over Los Angeles Dodgers in 4

There are two competing thoughts on best practices for predictions, and the above is an argument for following logic. No muss. No fuss. Just math, or something approximating math.

Then there's the notion that predictions are best served interesting . That's what we have with this NLCS pick, in which the Brewers would avenge their sweep at the hands of the Dodgers from last year.

No, Milwaukee can't hang with Los Angeles in a slug-fest. But unlike Yankees vs. Rays, the equalizer in this one is the Brewers' pitching. Jacob Misiorowski will be the best arm on either side, and some metrics rate Logan Henderson ahead of even Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto.

Milwaukee Brewers over New York Yankees in 7

The Brewers cost $165.8 million. They're David, clearly. The Yankees cost $338.6 million. They're Goliath, just as clearly.

Once everything moves between the white lines, though, it's only the quality of the baseball that matters. And in case anyone needs a reminder, the Brewers won 10 more games than the Yankees this season.

What the Yankees would have going for them is the model. As with all its other matchups, the long ball forecast favors New York. Even with only 18 from Aaron Judge, it hit 69 more home runs than Milwaukee during the regular season.

Yet if any team is going to run an end-around the "Only Home Runs Win in October" decree, it's the Brewers. They outscored the Yankees this season because they did everything else besides hit home runs. They especially hit a ton of doubles (279) and stole a ton of bases (162). Nobody converted baserunners into runs like they did.

If it is the whiff that must decide this series, so be it. Brewers pitchers can play that game better than the Yankees' staff can, and they have a trump card. Their pitchers had by far the highest whiff rate (28.7) on four-seam fastballs. Yankees hitters had a bottom-10 whiff rate (23.2) against four-seam fastballs.

As of now, the Yankees have the Brewers beat in all-time World Series championships 27-0. So, go ahead and score a big one for David.

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Every MLB Team's Biggest Surprise and Disappointment in 2026
articles.summary: Labeling an MLB player's season as a surprise or a disappointment is all about production relative to expectations.
articles.body:
Labeling an MLB player's season as a surprise or a disappointment is all about production relative to expectations.

A 30-year-old journeyman making a bigger-than-expected impact can be the biggest surprise on a roster, even if he wasn't the brightest star or player who received significant national attention.

On the flip side, a disappointing performance means legitimate expectations were not met, specifically by a player who has proved capable of a higher level of production in the past.

With the regular season completed, we've identified the biggest surprise and biggest disappointment for every MLB team in 2026.

Note: All stats reflect players' production with the team they are representing only.

Stats: 152 G, 122 OPS+, .255/.331/.475, 56 XBH (30 HR), 86 RBI WAR: 3.4

The Cardinals chipped in $31 million of the $42 million remaining on Arenado's contract to facilitate his trade to the D-backs in January, which gives a good indication of where expectations were at entering the 2026 season. The 35-year-old turned in his first 30-homer season since 2022, a year after logging a career-worst 89 OPS+ and 1.3 WAR in 107 games.

Stats: 20 GS, 3-9, 6.07 ERA, 1.55 WHIP, 64 K, 105.1 IP WAR: -1.7

After a disappointing contract year in 2025 that ended with a solid stretch of starts, Gallen returned to the D-backs on a one-year, $22.025 million deal after rejecting a qualifying offer at the start of the offseason. That means not only did they pay a steep price for his ugly 6.07 ERA, but they also gave up the opportunity to secure an additional draft pick if he signed elsewhere.

Stats: 111 G, 116 OPS+, .256/.322/.475, 40 XBH (22 HR), 16 SB WAR: 3.5

Gelof looked like a long-term building block when he racked up 2.5 WAR over 69 games as a rookie in 2023, but he followed that up with a .211 average and AL-leading 188 strikeouts the following year before an injury-plagued 2025 campaign. He started the 2026 season at Triple-A, but ended it as one of the few bright spots on the roster, alongside right-hander J.T. Ginn, who also deserves a mention here.

Biggest Disappointment: SP Jeffrey Springs

Stats: 29 GS, 4-14, 6.18 ERA, 1.47 WHIP, 112 K, 142.2 IP WAR: -0.5

With a solid track record of mid-level production, including a 4.11 ERA and 105 ERA+ over 171 innings in 2025, Springs looked like one of the few stable arms on the Athletics staff and earned the Opening Day start. With a 6.18 ERA, similarly rough 6.02 FIP and an AL-leading 35 home runs allowed, his season devolved into a disaster.

Stats: 26 GS, 9-9, 3.04 ERA, 1.28 WHIP, 102 K, 142.0 IP WAR: 2.9

The Braves signed Pérez to a minor league deal during the offseason and even floated him through a DFA/re-signing stretch before he settled in as one of the most reliable starters on a banged-up staff. At a modest $3.5 million price tag, he finished second among Braves pitchers with 2.9 WAR.

Stats: 51 G, 2 OPS+, .116/.219/.140, 2 XBH (0 HR), 2 SB WAR: -0.8

The Braves re-signed Kim to a one-year, $20 million deal during the offseason to serve as the primary shortstop, but a torn tendon in his finger from falling on ice and the lingering effects of that injury ended up limiting him to 51 games. An injury-shortened season is not automatically a disappointing one, but his production was so non-existent when he did take the field it's hard not to zero in on his 2 OPS+ in 147 plate appearances.

What's Next for Cubs After Playoff Exit? 📝

Stats: 28 GS, 9-6, 3.56 ERA, 1.35 WHIP, 133 K, 156.2 IP WAR: 2.3

A 27-year-old with a 6.24 ERA over 57.2 career innings heading into the 2026 season, Young opened the year at Triple-A and ended as Baltimore's WAR leader among pitchers. His 4.47 FIP and modest 19.9 percent strikeout rate limit his long-term upside, but he brought some much-needed stability to the staff in 2026.

Biggest Disappointment: OF Dylan Beavers

Stats: 104 G, 93 OPS+, .228/.307/.373, 29 XBH (9 HR), 44 RBI WAR: -0.5

After posting a 121 OPS+ with 10 extra-base hits and 1.0 WAR in 35 games in his first big league action down the stretch in 2025, Beavers was expected to be a key contributor in the Baltimore outfield. Instead, his on-base percentage cratered (.375 to .307), and poor defensive metrics (-8 DRS, -9 OAA) further drove down his overall value.

Stats: 29 GS, 18-5, 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 149 K, 169.0 IP

Entering his age-36 season and coming off a year where he logged a 4.28 ERA in 180.2 innings, Gray profiled as a middle-of-the-rotation innings eater when he was acquired from the Cardinals in November. Instead, he is likely headed for a top-five finish in AL Cy Young balloting, and he served as Boston's de facto ace after Garrett Crochet was sidelined.

Stats: 151 G, 76 OPS+, .207/.266/.361, 40 XBH (20 HR), 21 SB

There have been 527 individual 20/20 seasons in MLB history, and Duran's 0.4 WAR this year is tied for 519th among them. The counting statistics still point to some offensive value, but his overall production and defensive value declined sharply. He has fallen well short of both his 9.0-WAR peak two years ago and his 4.9-WAR campaign in 2025.

Biggest Surprise: OF/DH Michael Conforto

Stats: 113 G, 118 OPS+, .240/.331/.469, 32 XBH (15 HR), 45 RBI WAR: 0.7

The Cubs brought Dylan Carlson, Chas McCormick and Conforto to spring training looking to fill out the bench. A year after struggling to a .199 batting average and negative-0.7 WAR in 138 games for the Dodgers, Conforto ended up being a wildly productive part-time player, logging 314 plate appearances for a playoff contender while playing on a one-year, $2 million deal.

Shoutout to David Peterson (15 GS, 3.70 ERA, 80.1 IP), who was one of the better in-season bargain pickups across baseball.

Biggest Disappointment: SP Edward Cabrera

Stats: 15 GS, 5-5, 5.96 ERA, 1.49 WHIP, 71 K, 80.0 IP WAR: -1.4

The Cubs paid a steep price to acquire Cabrera from the Marlins during the offseason, sending a package headlined by top prospect Owen Caissie the other way in exchange for his three remaining years of club control. Coming off a 2025 season where he logged a 3.53 ERA and 150 strikeouts in 137.2 innings, his command regressed (8.3 to 10.3 BB%) and he was eventually relegated to the bullpen.

Stats: 156 G, 116 OPS+, .265/.337/.437, 47 XBH (12 HR), 56 RBI WAR: 3.6

Acquired from the Rays in December in exchange for cash considerations, Peters ended up playing his way onto the Opening Day roster, seizing the starting center field job and massively outplaying the departed Luis Robert Jr. in 2026. He was an All-Star and played Gold Glove-caliber defense (5 DRS, 11 OAA).

Biggest Disappointment: SP Luis Castillo

Stats: 9 G, 6 GS, 8.42 ERA, 1.81 WHIP, 26 K, 31.0 IP WAR: -0.9

The White Sox bought low on Castillo at the trade deadline hoping to add a veteran workhorse to their starting rotation for the stretch run, even if he was no longer the frontline starter he was in his prime. After serving up a 7.52 ERA in 26.1 innings over six starts, he was demoted to the bullpen and ultimately left off the Wild Card Series roster.

Stats: 133 G, 105 OPS+, .217/.324/.416, 43 XBH (24 HR), 58 RBI WAR: 1.2

After being non-tendered by the Athletics to start the offseason, Bleday signed a minor league deal with the Reds and started the year at Triple-A Louisville. He was recalled on April 26 and went on to win NL Player of the Month honors in May (1.018 OPS, 17 XBH, 8 HR, 25 RBI). He also hit for the cycle on Aug. 22 against the D-backs, more than delivering on his $1.85 million salary.

Stats: 63 G, 51 OPS+, .189/.229/.321, 13 XBH (6 HR), 15 RBI WAR: -1.5

There is no shortage of candidates for the Reds, including a poor contract year from Brady Singer, a disappointing reunion with Eugenio Suárez and a historically awful offensive showing from Ke'Bryan Hayes. However, Marte was trending toward being a legitimate long-term piece in 2025 with a 104 OPS+ and 1.4 WAR in 90 games, so his massive step backward in his age-24 season has bigger long-term ramifications.

Stats: 114 G, 110 OPS+, .254/.290/.465, 44 XBH (18 HR), 11 SB

After finishing with a 74 OPS+ and negative-0.7 WAR in 139 games during the 2025 season, Martínez was not even guaranteed a big league roster spot entering the 2026 season. A 106-point jump in his slugging percentage and a team-high 18 home runs qualify him as a massive surprise, even if his sub-.300 on-base percentage still left something to be desired.

Biggest Disappointment: 1B Kyle Manzardo

Stats: 102 G, 93 OPS+, .215/.306/.378, 24 XBH (13 HR), 39 RBI

Manzardo served as the primary lineup protection for José Ramírez during the 2025 season, posting a 111 OPS+ with 27 home runs and 70 RBI in a breakout year offensively. That production regressed to the point that he was demoted to Triple-A this year, and the Guardians went with deadline pickup Nathaniel Lowe as their primary first baseman down the stretch while chasing a division title.

Stats: 155 G, 121 OPS+, .300/.390/.453, 49 XBH (16 HR), 73 RBI WAR: 3.5

The Rockies acquired Rumfield from the Yankees in exchange for reliever Angel Chivilli in January and thrust him into a wide-open competition for the starting first base job. The 26-year-old rookie finished as the team leader in WAR (3.5), NL leader in on-base percentage (.390) and one of only seven qualified hitters with a .300 batting average.

Biggest Disappointment: SS Ezequiel Tovar

Stats: 146 G, 60 OPS+, .219/.264/.353, 36 XBH (13 HR), 44 RBI WAR: -0.3

Fully healthy following an injury-plagued 2025 season, Tovar failed to return to his 2024 form, when he racked up 75 extra-base hits and 3.6 WAR while winning NL Gold Glove honors. His 60 OPS+ ranked dead last among the 135 hitters who qualified for the batting title, miles behind No. 134 on that list, Marcus Semien (74 OPS+).

Stats: 20 GS, 8-5, 2.76 ERA, 1.13 WHIP, 94 K, 114.1 IP WAR: 2.8

Melton showed quality stuff down the stretch in 2025, but his role was unclear entering the year with Tarik Skubal, Framber Valdez, Jack Flaherty, Justin Verlander and Casey Mize penciled into the Detroit rotation. On the other side of injuries and trades, he was arguably the team's best pitcher, and he had a 1.86 ERA in 97 innings entering September before running out of gas down the stretch.

Biggest Disappointment: IF/OF Zach McKinstry

Stats: 129 G, 64 OPS+, .199/.288/.294, 23 XBH (4 HR), 26 RBI WAR: 1.7

An All-Star and Silver Slugger winner in 2025 as one of the game's best utility players, McKinstry provided plenty of value with his glove while continuing to play all over the field. However, his OPS plummeted from .771 to .582, essentially turning him into a glove-only option.

Stats: 29 GS, 8-10, 3.82 ERA, 1.25 WHIP, 154 K, 155.2 IP WAR: 3.1

After flashing some potential while navigating injuries during his time with the Rockies, Lambert put together a strong season for the Tokyo Yakult Swallows in 2025. The Astros signed him to a minor league deal, which he initially opted out of before re-signing a few days later, and he ended up leading the team in innings pitched (155.2) while backing his 3.82 ERA with an equally solid 3.91 FIP.

Stats: 17 GS, 4-9, 5.99 ERA, 1.55 WHIP, 75 K, 94.2 IP WAR: -1.0

The Astros gave up two high-profile prospects in Jacob Melton and Anderson Brito to acquire Burrows in a three-team deal with the Pirates and Rays. He was demoted to Triple-A in early July after a brutal outing against the Nationals (4.1 IP, 9 H, 10 R, 7 ER) and did not return to the MLB roster.

Stats: 13 GS, 3-5, 3.51 ERA, 1.40 WHIP, 49 K, 74.1 IP WAR: 1.3

A productive member of the Twins rotation once upon a time, Dobnak did not appear in the majors in 2022 or 2023 before tossing a combined 15 innings in the big leagues in 2024 and 2025. The Royals acquired him from the Mariners in June for cash considerations, and he ended up being a useful piece of a banged up starting rotation.

Stats: 32 GS, 7-9, 5.17 ERA, 1.47 WHIP, 134 K, 172.1 IP WAR: -0.3

Two years removed from a runner-up finish in AL Cy Young balloting, Lugo served up an AL-leading 200 hits and 99 earned runs while logging just 14 quality starts in 32 outings. Opponents hit a combined .295/.352/.480 against him, and the Royals finished 16-16 in games he started.

Stats: 98 G, 119 OPS+, .300/.373/.387, 19 XBH (3 HR), 8 SB WAR: 2.4

After making his MLB debut during the second half of the 2023 season, Meckler did not see the big leagues in the two years that followed, and the Angels claimed him off waivers in January. He was recalled from the minors on May 22, and needed just 98 games to finish third in WAR among Angels position players.

Stats: 75 G, 63 OPS+, .209/.271/.295, 12 XBH (4 HR), 23 RBI WAR: -1.0

O'Hoppe looked like a long-term piece for the Angels during a 2.7-WAR, 20-homer season in 2024. His offense and defense both regressed in 2025, and he struggled to the point of being demoted to the minors this year before he was traded to the Rangers at the deadline.

Stats: 61 G, 11 HLD, 2.85 ERA, 1.03 WHIP, 71 K, 60.0 IP WAR: 0.8

With a fastball that averages 100.7 mph and a slider that has generated a 43.2 percent whiff rate, Henriquez has showcased electric stuff since his time in the minors. The surprise is that he has been such an integral part of the Dodgers' relief corps, joining Alex Vesia and Tanner Scott as one of the team's most reliable late-inning options.

Stats: 154 G, 97 OPS+, .233/.330/.385, 44 XBH (17 HR), 12 SB WAR: 0.7

Living up to a four-year, $240 million contract was never going to be easy, but Tucker fell short of even league-average production in his Dodgers debut. The numbers actually looked even worse before a productive final month, as he entered September with a .228/.326/.357 line and 11 home runs in 129 games.

Stats: 157 G, 122 OPS+, .305/.349/.437, 52 XBH (11 HR), 34 SB WAR: 6.1

A breakout offensive season alongside his usual standout defense made Lopez one of the most valuable shortstops in baseball, with his 6.1 WAR behind only Kevin McGonigle (7.1) and Bobby Witt Jr. (6.7) at the position. After hitting .246/.305/.368 a year ago, he was the NL hits leader (191) and a contender for the NL batting title into the final month.

Biggest Disappointment: C Agustín Ramírez

Stats: 72 G, 91 OPS+, .235/.318/.354, 16 XBH (5 HR), 24 RBI WAR: -0.3

Ramírez slugged 33 doubles and 21 home runs as a rookie in 2025, but his poor defense and .287 on-base percentage made him a negative-WAR player overall. A less potent start at the plate and the arrival of top catching prospect Joe Mack led to him spending much of 2026 back at Triple-A.

Stats: 144 G, 140 OPS+, .266/.389/.484, 50 XBH (26 HR), 86 RBI WAR: 3.3

A .211/.307/.365 career hitter entering 2026, Bauers had never hit more than 12 home runs while serving mostly as a platoon player. This year's offensive outburst has been accompanied by some of the best batted-ball metrics of any hitter in baseball, and his career year lined up perfectly with his first trip to free agency this winter.

Stats: 111 G, 70 OPS+, .230/.295/.319, 22 XBH (4 HR), 7 SB WAR: -0.5

With a 111 OPS+ and 2.9 WAR in 142 games during the 2025 season, Frelick looked like a foundational piece on the rise for the Brewers with potential for more heading into the year. Instead, he struggled mightily before suffering a torn labrum in July, and after missing a month he returned to a part-time role with Luis Lara absorbing some of his playing time in right field.

Stats: 31 GS, 12-6, 3.73 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 205 K, 178.1 IP

The Twins bought low on Bradley at the 2025 trade deadline, acquiring him in exchange for Griffin Jax after he had been demoted to the minors. He was shelled in six starts after the trade (6.61 ERA, 31.1 IP), but the move paid major dividends this season as he pitched his way into the co-ace role alongside Joe Ryan. Still only 25 years old, he is controllable through 2029.

Stats: 34 G, 55 OPS+, .167/.259/.292, 7 XBH (4 HR), 10 RBI

After posting a 112 OPS+ with 22 home runs in 104 games in 2025, Wallner was the starting right fielder and No. 5 hitter for the Twins on Opening Day. His .167 average and 39.3 percent strikeout rate earned him a demotion to the minors in mid-May, and he never returned, spending 94 games at Triple-A St. Paul.

Stats: 103 G, 113 OPS+, .266/.330/.429, 29 XBH (9 HR), 39 RBI WAR: 1.7

Young entered the 2026 season with 44 MLB games under his belt and a .200/.267/.457 batting line over 116 plate appearances. Exactly who the Mets would turn to as they looked for a Pete Alonso replacement, right? With free-agent signing Jorge Polanco sidelined for most of the year, Young played his way into regular action at first base and ended up being one of the team's most productive bats.

Biggest Disappointment: SP Freddy Peralta

Stats: 22 GS, 5-9, 4.99 ERA, 1.48 WHIP, 113 K, 113.2 IP WAR: -0.5

Acquired to front the starting rotation alongside rising ace Nolan McLean, Peralta was coming off arguably the best season of his career. In 2025, he finished 17-6 with a 2.70 ERA, 1.08 WHIP and 204 strikeouts in 176.2 innings, earning a fifth-place finish in NL Cy Young balloting. The Mets ended up cutting their losses at the deadline, and he immediately righted the ship with a 3.25 ERA in 55.1 innings in Tampa Bay.

Stats: 81 G, 29 HLD, 2.18 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 98 K, 78.1 IP WAR: 2.6

The Yankees finished second in the majors with a 3.13 ERA from the relief corps, and Headrick was a huge part of their success. The 28-year-old had a 4.70 ERA over 32 appearances during sporadic MLB action the previous three seasons, but emerged as one of the most dominant lefty setup men in baseball.

Tip of the cap to Paul Blackburn (62 G, 11 HLD, 1.69 ERA, 85.0 IP), as the longtime starter reinvented himself as a lights-out bullpen option.

Biggest Disappointment: 2B Jazz Chisholm Jr.

Stats: 137 G, 97 OPS+, .231/.312/.399, 38 XBH (19 HR), 41 SB WAR: 1.7

The numbers aren't terrible at first glance, but they were a significant step backward from Chisholm after he logged a 122 OPS+ with 31 home runs, 31 steals and 4.1 WAR in 2025. The 28-year-old's regression came at a less-than-ideal time with free agency looming this winter.

Stats: 67 G, 107 OPS+, .261/.296/.487, 12 XBH (7 HR), 6 SB

A first-round pick in 2014 who never lived up to expectations in Detroit, Hill has bounced around a ton the last few seasons. After Adolis García suffered a season-ending injury, the Phillies acquired him from the White Sox in June. Hill ended up settling nicely into the fourth outfielder role, carving out some platoon work thanks to a .781 OPS against southpaws.

Stats: 157 G, 81 OPS+, .242/.297/.378, 49 XBH (19 HR), 21 SB

It has been an up-and-down four years in Philadelphia for Turner, but he was coming off a fantastic 2025 season where he hit .304/.355/.457 with 5.4 WAR in 141 games to win the NL batting title and finish fifth in NL MVP balloting. He started 154 games at shortstop, but the turnaround simply never came in a negative-WAR campaign.

Stats: 70 G, 18 SV, 2.88 ERA, 1.03 WHIP, 105 K, 68.2 IP WAR: 2.4

The Pirates acquired Brandon Lowe, Jake Mangum and Montgomery from the Rays last offseason in a three-team, six-player deal that sent Mike Burrows to the Astros. Montgomery pitched to a 5.67 ERA in 57 games as a rookie in 2025, but his 12.3 K/9 spoke to the quality of his stuff. A year later, he was one of the most overpowering bullpen arms in baseball, pitching his way into the closer's role while setting a franchise record with 25 straight scoreless appearances.

Biggest Disappointment: DH Marcell Ozuna

Stats: 70 G, 67 OPS+, .203/.286/.327, 15 XBH (8 HR), 29 RBI WAR: -1.0

Signed to add some middle-of-the-order thump, Ozuna's one-year, $10.5 million deal made him the sixth-highest-paid player on the Pirates roster. He went 2-for-39 in his first 10 games and never really recovered, and he was ultimately released on Aug. 6.

Stats: 133 G, 139 OPS+, .295/.363/.502, 47 XBH (21 HR), 72 RBI WAR: 4.5

France signed a minor league deal in February, rejoining the franchise that originally selected him in the 34th round of the 2015 draft. He played his way onto the Opening Day roster and into a regular role at first base, putting together the best season of his career in multiple categories. His 4.5 WAR trailed only Pete Alonso (4.9) and Willson Contreras (4.6) among first basemen, bolstered by his Gold Glove-caliber defense.

Stats: 10 GS, 2-4, 7.46 ERA, 1.68 WHIP, 25 K, 44.2 IP WAR: -1.3

The Padres paid a steep price for a two-month rental of Mize, who had a 2.70 ERA, 0.99 WHIP and 85 strikeouts in 86.2 innings with the Tigers prior to the trade. Expected to help solidify the top of the starting rotation, he was shelled for nine hits and eight earned runs in 3.1 innings in his Padres debut and never settled in with his new team.

Stats: 105 G, 127 OPS+, .324/.360/.440, 34 XBH (4 HR), 43 RBI WAR: 3.0

The offensive production is not the major surprise here, though Arraez did improve on a 101 OPS+ during the 2025 season. The surprise was his strong defensive metrics at second base (1,275.1 INN, 12 OAA), after the Giants were the only team willing to give him a shot at being an everyday guy there during the offseason. That should help bolster his market this winter after he settled for a one-year, $12 million deal last time around.

Biggest Disappointment: OF Harrison Bader

Stats: 30 G, 54 OPS+, .170/.198/.358, 10 XBH (5 HR), 14 RBI WAR: 0.2

For the most part, players have been given a pass from the biggest disappointments section if their season was cut short due to injury. However, the circumstances surrounding Bader's injury make him a worthy exception, and there's a very real chance he has played his final game in a Giants uniform, despite signing a two-year, $20.5 million deal last winter.

Stats: 25 GS, 7-8, 3.57 ERA, 1.14 WHIP, 126 K, 138.2 IP WAR: 2.7

Hancock only earned a spot in Seattle's Opening Day rotation because Bryce Miller was sidelined to start the year, but he tossed six no-hit innings in his first start of the year and never relinquished his starting role. The 27-year-old had the track record as the No. 6 overall pick in the 2020 draft, but with a 4.81 ERA in 162.2 career innings entering the year he had previously looked more like organizational depth than an impact starter.

Stats: 126 G, 91 OPS+, .182/.296/.368, 38 XBH (23 HR), 69 RBI WAR: 1.0

The numbers looked even worse for Raleigh before he slugged nine home runs in August, but he still saw his production absolutely fall off a cliff relative to his 60-homer, 7.2-WAR season in 2025. With four years left on his six-year, $105 million extension, the M's will be counting on him returning to star-level production next season.

Stats: 158 G, 124 OPS+, .269/.327/.466, 62 XBH (29 HR), 102 RBI WAR: 3.3

Despite being only 24 years old, Walker was entering a make-or-break season of sorts after hitting a combined .211/.270/.324 for a 69 OPS+ and negative-2.5 WAR over 162 games in 2024 and 2025. He stumbled down the stretch, hitting .172 with a .519 OPS in September, but he has firmly established himself as a piece to build around.

Biggest Disappointment: SP Matthew Liberatore

Stats: 31 GS, 6-14, 5.23 ERA, 1.47 WHIP, 154 K, 155.0 IP WAR: -0.6

Liberatore turned in an under-the-radar breakout season in 2025 with a 4.21 ERA in 151.2 innings, and the Cardinals handed him the ball on Opening Day. The 26-year-old had 10 starts where he allowed one or zero earned runs, so there were still flashes of his rotation anchor potential, but they were accompanied by seven starts where he served up five or more earned runs.

Stats: 65 G, 41 SV, 1.44 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 63 K, 62.1 IP WAR: 2.9

After declining their club option on Pete Fairbanks last winter, the Rays entered the season without a set closer. By season's end, Baker was tied for the MLB lead with 41 saves, using a lethal fastball-changeup combination to turn in a season that should earn him Mariano Rivera AL Reliever of the Year honors. The 31-year-old was acquired from the Orioles midway through the 2025 season.

Biggest Disappointment: RP Garrett Cleavinger

Stats: 51 G, 2 SV, 23 HLD, 4.79 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 54 K, 41.1 IP WAR: -0.3

It was Cleavinger who was the breakout arm in the Tampa Bay bullpen last year when he logged a 2.35 ERA and 12.0 K/9 in 67 appearances. That even earned him a spot on Team USA in the World Baseball Classic. With two saves and 23 holds, he still filled a high-leverage role, but the end result was a significant step backward.

Stats: 58 G, 30 SV, 2.13 ERA, 0.81 WHIP, 83 K, 72.0 IP WAR: 2.6

Latz landed in the Texas bullpen after losing the No. 5 starter battle to Kumar Rocker during spring training, and by midseason he was at the All-Star Game as one of baseball's best closers. He allowed just 35 hits in 72 innings en route to a .143 opponents' batting average.

A 4.2-WAR season from Ezequiel Durán in a super-utility role has to at least be mentioned, though he has been productive in the past, making Latz's performance far more surprising.

Stats: 141 G, 76 OPS+, .194/.288/.315, 26 XBH (9 HR), 17 SB WAR: 1.9

Health was the question mark for Carter in 2024 (45 games) and 2025 (63 games), and he continued to flash star potential with a 110 OPS+ and 1.9 WAR when he was healthy a year ago. This season, he played a career-high 141 games, but was one of the least productive regulars in baseball, ranking in the 10th percentile or worse in expected average and expected slugging.

Stats: 41 G, 129 OPS+, .329/.402/.424, 10 XBH (2 HR), 3 SB WAR: 2.2

Bateman never ranked higher than the No. 30 prospect in the Cubs farm system, but he was plugged in as Toronto's starting center fielder after he was acquired in the Kevin Gausman deal, replacing fellow trade chip Daulton Varsho. His performance should be enough to secure him a starting job in 2027, especially with his defense (6 DRS, 3 OAA) providing a strong foundation.

Biggest Disappointment: 1B Vladimir Guerrero Jr.

Stats: 144 G, 90 OPS+, .260/.332/.356, 34 XBH (9 HR), 57 RBI WAR: 1.1

Signed to a 14-year, $500 million extension last year, Guerrero put together an all-time postseason performance with a .397/.494/.795 line and eight home runs in 18 games. His power completely disappeared this season en route to the worst offensive numbers of his career, and ill-advised comments regarding his contract ended his down year on a particularly sour note.

Stats: 25 G, 17 GS, 2-6, 3.43 ERA, 1.30 WHIP, 114 K, 112.2 IP WAR: 2.5

First used as a multi-inning reliever and then as a swingman, Alvarez eventually assumed a regular spot in the Nationals rotation in August. Over the final two months, he had a 2.78 ERA and 56 strikeouts in 55 innings. The 27-year-old rookie can fill a variety of roles going forward.

Stats: 95 G, 95 OPS+, .247/.313/.397, 28 XBH (10 HR), 46 RBI WAR: 0.7

House entered the regular season with some legitimate breakout expectations after he hit .429/.444/.786 with six doubles, three home runs and 11 RBI during spring training. By May 19, he had been optioned back to Triple-A, and even at 23 years old he is quickly approaching make-or-break territory if he is going to stake his claim as the everyday third baseman.

articles.title: Ranking Phillies 2B Luis Arraez's Top 5 Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: Any club pursuing three-time batting champion Luis Arraez will likely need a plan to play him regularly at second base.
articles.body:
Any club pursuing three-time batting champion Luis Arraez will likely need a plan to play him regularly at second base.

In a 2026 season split between the San Francisco Giants and Philadelphia Phillies, Arraez returned to his natural position of second base. In terms of outs above average, he had the best season of his career, with San Francisco infield coach Ron Washington credited with helping his defensive growth.

Arraez should do better this offseason than the one-year, $12 million deal he settled for last offseason. He was unavailable for the Phillies' Wild Card Series loss to Atlanta because of a sprained left ankle, though the injury is not expected to affect his availability for 2027.

Let's take a look at the best potential landing spots for the four-time All-Star.

Whether the Rangers are in on Arraez will depend on whether managing partner Ray Davis authorizes president of baseball operations Chris Young to add payroll in the offseason.

From a baseball perspective, the Rangers' second basemen posted an OPS south of .700 this season. Clearly, Arraez would give them more offensively than they got in 2026.

Top prospect Sebastian Walcott is a shortstop/third baseman who is expected to play a role for the team in 2027. But even with Corey Seager at shortstop and Josh Jung at third base, Walcott seems more likely to play outfield than second base. There aren't many 6'4" second basemen.

Arraez didn't perform as well with the Phillies as he did with the Giants, but his track record suggests that over a larger sample size, he will hit for a higher average.

The Phillies dealt pitching prospects Ramon Marquez and Marty Gair to acquire Arraez and reliever Caleb Kilian, so they should at least consider a reunion in free agency.

That said, some of this will come down to how the Phillies want to set up their infield in 2027. Alec Bohm will likely depart in free agency, while Bryce Harper is expected to return to first base.

Will the Phillies move Trea Turner off of shortstop, and if so will that be to second base or left field? What about Bryson Stott, whom the team likes at second base but moved to third to accommodate Arraez? Also looming is top prospect Aidan Miller, who missed most of 2026 but is an exciting bat who can play shortstop or third base.

Many moving parts make it unclear whether the Phillies will commit to multiple seasons of Arraez at second base. Still, his presence behind Bryce Harper gave Philadelphia a contact-oriented option in the heart of its lineup and may have made it easier for Harper to remain selective at the plate.

Will the Pirates extend the qualifying offer to Brandon Lowe? It's always difficult to know how owner Bob Nutting will operate. Even if the QO goes to Lowe, one would think he'd decline it in search of a multi-year commitment.

If Lowe ends up not returning to Pittsburgh, the Buccos will have a hole at second base. One way to soften the negative reaction to not bringing Lowe back after an excellent contract year is to sign a replacement as accomplished as Arraez.

You could do worse than a middle-infield pairing of Arraez and Konnor Griffin, especially in terms of offensive production.

It's rare but not unheard of for a player to get traded midseason and then return to the club that traded him in the offseason as a free agent. This might be one of the instances where it makes sense, though.

Arraez not only built a great relationship with the aforementioned Washington, but he also hit .324 in 105 games with the Giants. While home run hitters other than Barry Bonds don't love Oracle Park, Arraez's offensive profile fit the park well. In 49 games at Oracle Park in 2026, Arraez hit .361.

This may come down to whether the Giants are comfortable with Casey Schmitt playing elsewhere on the diamond so Arraez can resume as the team's second baseman. Offensively, Arraez remains a great fit for the Giants.

The Tigers will have quite a bit of money coming off the books this offseason, including the $22.025 million that Gleyber Torres made after accepting the qualifying offer last winter.

Arraez spent the first four seasons of his career with the Minnesota Twins, so a return to the AL Central could make sense. It's a bit surprising that Arraez has hit only .265 in 88 career plate appearances at Comerica Park, but the spacious outfield suits a contact hitter.

Additionally, with Torres coming off the books, the Tigers will have an opening at second base. Adding Arraez's bat-to-ball skills could help Detroit rebound from a disappointing 2026.

articles.title: New Aaron Judge Rumors, Updated Injury Status for Yankees vs. Rays in 2026 MLB Playoffs
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays may have to wait until closer to Saturday's first pitch of the ALDS to find out if Game 1 starter Drew Rasmussen will be facing Aaron Judge at the plate, ESPN's Jeff Passan reported Friday.
articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Rays may have to wait until closer to Saturday's first pitch of the ALDS to find out if Game 1 starter Drew Rasmussen will be facing Aaron Judge at the plate, ESPN's Jeff Passan reported Friday.

As of Friday morning, Passan reported Judge's status "remains up in the air and is unlikely to be decided until shortly before the series begins Saturday, sources familiar with the deliberations told ESPN."

"Some in the organization want him to play," Passan reported. "Others, wary of him further aggravating the injury and imperiling him for the remainder of the postseason, would prefer to wait another week."

Passan noted the decision is also impacted by the fact Judge could be returning as a designated hitter. Notably, DH Luis García Jr. just helped the Yankees close out their Wild Card sweep of the Boston Red Sox by opening Game 2 scoring with a home run.

Judge initially said he hoped to return for the beginning of the postseason before he was left off the Yankees' Wild Card roster amid his recovery from the right calf strain that resulted in a trip to the injured list on Sept. 19.

Yankees manager Aaron Boone said at the time the decision was made because the club didn't feel Judge was "all the way back."

Judge has appeared in just seven games for the Yankees since he was shut down with a right rib injury May 31. Following his return Sept. 8, he was held to a batting average of .174 with one home run in 24 plate appearances before suffering the calf injury.

The Yankees will hope giving Judge more time to recover from his latest injury will result in a more productive return from the slugger. Should he sit out the divisional series, he would gain an additional week to recover in the event the Yankees advance to the ALCS.

Gerrit Cole will start Game 1 for the Yankees when the ALDS begins Saturday at 6:30 p.m. ET in St. Petersburg. He will be facing a more rested lineup given that the Rays sat out the Wild Card round after clinching the AL's top seed.
